modules.default_title: Lipid Management — CV Risk & Statin Prescribing
modules.landing_intro: Clinical decision support for lipid management and cardiovascular risk reduction in primary care. Use this module when initiating statin therapy, reviewing a patient not at LDL goal, or counseling a statin-hesitant patient. Content reflects the 2026 ACC/AHA Multisociety Dyslipidemia Guideline, which formally adopts AHA PREVENT for ages 30–79 in place of the Pooled Cohort Equations, lowers risk-tier thresholds to preserve statin eligibility across diverse populations, and reinstates LDL-C and non-HDL-C as co-primary treatment targets. The 2022 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway is retained for nonstatin-therapy operational specifics.

context_strip.label: Organizational and Tool Context
context_strip.text: AHA PREVENT-ASCVD is the required risk-stratification tool for statin decisions in primary care, replacing the Pooled Cohort Equations.[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:khan-circ-2024] PREVENT total-CVD (ASCVD + heart failure) applies to blood-pressure decisions under the 2025 BP guideline[ref:acc-aha-bp-2025] — not statin decisions. Until Epic BPA integration is live, calculate at acc.org/PREVENT.  Statin Use in Persons with Diabetes (SUPD) tracks pharmacy-claim dispensing for adults age 40–75 with diabetes. The Crystal Run organizational target of ~90% is an internal expectation, not the HEDIS national 90th percentile (~80–85% commercial). The HEDIS measure rewards dispensing — not chart documentation of the benefit-risk discussion — but local practice expectation is that statin therapy be addressed and documented at every diabetic visit, including when the patient declines.  Three controlled-substance modules and this lipid module share an evidence-rewrite pipeline. Any gap or correction should be reported via the feedback button.

faqs.title: Calculating ASCVD risk with PREVENT
faqs.first_layer_html:
The 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guideline formally adopts AHA PREVENT-ASCVD as the primary risk estimator for ages 30–79, replacing the Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE).[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc] The four risk tiers:

Thresholds were lowered from the legacy PCE tiers[ref:michos-nejm-2019] specifically so PREVENT identifies approximately the same number of statin-eligible adults (~25–26 million)[ref:diao-jama-2024]. Applying PREVENT to old PCE thresholds would have de-eligibilized ~14–17 million adults, disproportionately Black adults.[ref:diao-jama-2024][ref:anderson-jamaim-2024]

sub_questions.question: Why did PREVENT replace the Pooled Cohort Equations?
sub_questions.answer_html: PREVENT incorporates kidney function (eGFR) and metabolic context (diabetes, optionally HbA1c and UACR), removes race as an input, and is calibrated for ages 30–79 vs PCE's 40–75[ref:khan-circ-2024][ref:khan-circ-2023-aha-statement]. The PCE was found to broadly miscalibrate in contemporary populations — the largest absolute difference between PCE and PREVENT was in Black adults (10.9% PCE vs 5.1% PREVENT)[ref:anderson-jamaim-2024]. Base predictors: age, sex, total cholesterol, HDL-C, SBP, eGFR, diabetes, smoking, statin use, antihypertensive use. BMI is in the PREVENT-HF equation only — not PREVENT-ASCVD[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026].

sub_questions.question: What are the 2026 risk-enhancing factors?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Risk enhancers support statin initiation in borderline-risk patients (COR 2a)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. The 2026 list includes:

  • Family history of premature ASCVD
  • Higher-risk ancestry (South Asian, Filipino)
  • High polygenic risk score (when measured)
  • Chronic inflammatory disease (SLE, RA, advanced psoriasis)
  • Lp(a) ≥125 nmol/L (or ≥50 mg/dL)
  • hsCRP ≥2 mg/L on >1 occasion — 2 successive occasions in borderline tier specifically supports high-intensity statin (COR 2a, LOE B-R)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]
  • Triglycerides persistently ≥175 mg/dL nonfasting or ≥150 mg/dL fasting
  • CKM (cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic) syndrome
  • LDL-C persistently 160–189, non-HDL-C 190–219, or ApoB ≥120 mg/dL
  • Reproductive markers: premature menopause, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, gestational HTN, preterm delivery, early menarche

Note: ABI <0.9 is no longer a standalone risk enhancer — symptomatic PAD with ABI <0.85 is now captured under VHR major events[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]. The 2018 prerequisite of LDL ≥70 mg/dL at borderline is also removed.

sub_questions.question: My patient is 30–59 with low 10-year risk. Can I use PREVENT differently?
sub_questions.answer_html: Yes. Adults 30–59 with 10-year PREVENT <3% and 30-year PREVENT ≥10% may reasonably initiate a moderate-intensity statin (COR 2a, LOE C-LD)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]. LOE is limited — no RCTs in this specific cohort — and the guideline emphasizes a trial of health-behavior optimization first. For adults under 30 or over 79, PREVENT is not calibrated; use clinical judgment with risk-enhancing factors[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:khan-circ-2024].

sub_questions.question: A long-term statin patient now reclassifies lower under PREVENT. Do I de-escalate?
sub_questions.answer_html: Do not unilaterally de-escalate. Under the old PCE thresholds applied to PREVENT, ~4 million currently-treated adults would have lost statin eligibility[ref:anderson-jamaim-2024]. The 2026 ≥3% threshold was specifically designed to narrow that gap. The 2026 ACC/AHA guideline and the 2026 VA/DoD Lipid CPG both frame any de-escalation as a benefit-risk discussion[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:va-dod-lipid-2026] — not an automatic consequence of reclassification. Document the tier change, consider risk enhancers and CAC, and engage shared decision-making.

faqs.title: When and how to initiate statin therapy
faqs.first_layer_html:
Three COR 1 indications for statin initiation in 2026[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]:

  • PREVENT-ASCVD ≥10% — high-intensity statin, targeting ≥50% LDL-C reduction
  • LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL — high-intensity statin regardless of risk score; evaluate for FH (see [ldl-190])
  • Diabetes, age 40–75 — at minimum moderate-intensity statin[ref:ada-2026-cv]

For all indications — including COR 1 — statin initiation is a benefit-risk discussion. COR 1 means "should be done"; it does not mean "without conversation." Document the discussion, patient preference, and clinical factors that drove the decision.

sub_questions.question: When is a statin reasonable but not COR 1?
sub_questions.answer_html: Intermediate risk (5–<10%) is COR 1 in 2026 — a meaningful upgrade from prior guidelines where it was COR 2a[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. COR 2a indications include: borderline-risk (3–<5%) with risk enhancers; 30-year PREVENT ≥10% in adults 30–59 with low 10-year risk; CAC ≥1 in any tier (LOE B-NR); high-intensity statin in intermediate-risk patients with hsCRP ≥2 mg/L on 2 successive occasions (COR 2a, LOE B-R)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026].

sub_questions.question: What's the SUPD HEDIS expectation for my diabetes patients?
sub_questions.answer_html: See Context section for the Crystal Run organizational SUPD target (~90% pharmacy-claim dispensing) vs the HEDIS national benchmark (~80–85% commercial)[ref:ada-2026-cv]. Local practice expectation: statin therapy addressed and documented at every diabetic visit, including when the patient declines. This aligns with the 2026 guideline's COR 1 recommendation for at-minimum moderate-intensity statin in adults 40–75 with diabetes[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026].

sub_questions.question: What are the VHR criteria?
sub_questions.answer_html:
VHR = ≥2 major ASCVD events, OR 1 major ASCVD event + ≥2 high-risk conditions (the count is 2, not 1 — a "1 + 1" count under-classifies[ref:aha-acc-ccd-2023]).

Major ASCVD events: recent ACS within 12 months, prior MI, ischemic stroke, symptomatic PAD[ref:acc-2022-decisionpathway][ref:aha-acc-ccd-2023] with ABI <0.85 or prior revascularization/amputation.

High-risk conditions: age ≥65; HeFH; prior CABG or PCI outside the index event; diabetes mellitus; hypertension; current smoking; LDL-C ≥100 despite max statin + ezetimibe; history of CHF.

CKD note (2026 change): The 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guideline removes CKD from the VHR high-risk features list[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026] — a change from the 2022 ECDP and 2023 CCD. CKD + ASCVD patients still receive aggressive LDL-C goals (<55 mg/dL) via the CKD-specific pathway (Section 4.2.8); CKD no longer itself escalates VHR classification alongside the eight conditions above.

For VHR patients ≥75, high-intensity statin is appropriate at any age — the 2026 guideline removed the prior age ≤75 restriction[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. Don't de-escalate based on very-low achieved LDL alone.

sub_questions.question: Does the VHR vs non-VHR distinction still matter?
sub_questions.answer_html: For now, yes — but the 2026 writing committee has signaled that future revisions may collapse VHR vs non-VHR ASCVD into a single <55 mg/dL pathway, pending VESALIUS-CV trial results[ref:blumenthal-circ-2026-progress]. The 2026 COR 2a option to intensify non-VHR ASCVD to <55 is an early step. Module structure stays VHR-vs-non-VHR for now.

sub_questions.question: Is the <55 mg/dL target safe at very low achieved LDL-C?
sub_questions.answer_html: Yes. FOURIER prespecified secondary analysis showed no excess adverse events at LDL <0.5 mmol/L (~19 mg/dL)[ref:giugliano-lancet-2017]. EBBINGHAUS found no neurocognitive impairment with PCSK9 mAb at very low LDL[ref:rosenson-jacc-2018]. The AHA Statin Safety Scientific Statement found no association between aggressive LDL-C lowering and dementia, cognitive impairment, or hemorrhagic stroke[ref:newman-atvb-2019]. Median achieved LDL: FOURIER ~30 mg/dL; ODYSSEY OUTCOMES ~40 mg/dL; IMPROVE-IT ezetimibe arm ~53 mg/dL[ref:cannon-nejm-2015][ref:sabatine-jamacardio-2018].

faqs.title: LDL-C, non-HDL-C, ApoB, and Lp(a)
faqs.first_layer_html: The 2026 ACC/AHA guideline reinstates LDL-C and non-HDL-C as co-primary treatment targets across every risk tier[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]. Non-HDL-C (= total cholesterol − HDL-C) is available on every standard panel without fasting, captures all atherogenic apoB-containing lipoproteins[ref:raja-atherosclerosis-2023], and is more reliable than calculated LDL-C when triglycerides are elevated. For LDL-C estimation, Martin/Hopkins or Sampson/NIH equations outperform Friedewald in all patients (COR 1, LOE B-NR)[ref:sajja-jacc-2022][ref:sampson-jamacardio-2020] and should be used preferentially — particularly when TG is elevated.

sub_questions.question: When should I order ApoB?
sub_questions.answer_html:
ApoB is most useful once LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals are at or near target, to assess residual atherogenic burden. The 2026 recommendations:

  • COR 2a on lipid-lowering therapy — particularly with ASCVD, CKM syndrome, T2D, or TG ≥150 mg/dL — to guide further intensification after LDL-C/non-HDL-C goals are achieved[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]
  • COR 2b in untreated adults — to enhance risk assessment or characterize inherited lipid disorders, especially with FH suspicion or premature ASCVD family history

The 2026 ACC/AHA does not specify a universal numeric ApoB target. The only ACC/AHA-specified ApoB numeric is <55 mg/dL for severe hypercholesterolemia + ASCVD (Section 4.2.4.3). The widely-cited ApoB <65 mg/dL derives from ESC/EAS 2019, not 2026 ACC/AHA[ref:fegers-wustrow-jacc-2022] — do not attribute to these guidelines.

sub_questions.question: When should I order Lp(a) and how do I interpret it?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Lp(a) is COR 1 once-in-lifetime in every adult — a major upgrade from 2018, where elevated Lp(a) was a risk enhancer only[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc].

2026 risk thresholds (Table 4):

  • 75–124 nmol/L: ~1.2× risk
  • ≥125 nmol/L (≥50 mg/dL): ~1.4× risk
  • ≥250 nmol/L (≥100 mg/dL): ≥2× risk
  • ≥350 nmol/L: ~3× risk; ≥430 nmol/L: ~4× risk

Single measurement is sufficient in most patients — Lp(a) is predominantly genetically determined and stable. Document in the lifetime problem list. Note: the often-cited ≥175 nmol/L "very-high" threshold is from the EAS consensus, not 2026 ACC/AHA. Note also: mg/dL × ~2.5 ≈ nmol/L is approximate, not exact, due to apo(a) isoform size variation[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026].

sub_questions.question: How do current therapies affect Lp(a)?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Statins do not meaningfully lower Lp(a) — Xie 2025 meta-analysis (147 RCTs, 145,314 subjects) found a mean +1.1 mg/dL absolute change with no significant clinical effect[ref:xie-atherosclerosis-2025]. The often-cited "statins raise Lp(a) 10–15%" figure is not supported.

PCSK9 mAbs reduce Lp(a) ~26% pooled; inclisiran ~22%[ref:xie-atherosclerosis-2025][ref:qiao-drugs-2026]. For ASCVD patients with elevated Lp(a) not at LDL-C goal, the 2026 guideline directs toward a PCSK9 mAb with proven CV benefit (evolocumab, alirocumab) — driven by FOURIER/ODYSSEY outcomes evidence, not by the Lp(a) magnitude differential, which is directional but not statistically significant (Mulligan JCL 2026)[ref:mulligan-jcl-2026].

No FDA-approved Lp(a)-specific therapy is currently available. Investigational agents (pelacarsen, olpasiran, zerlasiran, lepodisiran, muvalaplin[ref:nordestgaard-lancet-2024][ref:malick-jacc-2023]) are in Phase 2–3 trials. Phase 3 outcomes trials (Lp(a)HORIZON, OCEAN(a), ALPACA) are pending.

sub_questions.question: Operationally, when and how do I order ApoB and Lp(a) at a visit?
sub_questions.answer_html: For adults without a prior Lp(a): order it once with the next routine lipid draw and document in the lifetime problem list. ApoB: most useful in patients on lipid-lowering therapy with ASCVD, CKM, T2D, or TG ≥150 mg/dL, once LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals are near target. Both tests are covered by most commercial and Medicare plans without prior authorization (some plans require a diagnosis code for Lp(a), e.g., E78.5). Out-of-pocket cost when uncovered: ~$20–60 ApoB / ~$30–80 Lp(a). Neither is auto-included in routine lipid panels — order specifically.

faqs.title: Statin selection, intensity, and monitoring
faqs.first_layer_html:
Documentation must include: statin name and intensity (low/moderate/high), whether the patient is at LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals, next step if not at goal, and follow-up interval. Order a lipid panel 4–12 weeks after initiation or any dose change, then every 6–12 months (COR 1, LOE A)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]. Fasting is not required in most cases — nonfasting is the default unless the patient has known hypertriglyceridemia.

sub_questions.question: Should I order liver enzymes or CK on routine statin monitoring?
sub_questions.answer_html: Routine ALT monitoring on stable statin therapy is COR 3 No Benefit (LOE B-NR)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. The 2026 follow-up recommendation specifies a lipid profile only at 4–12 weeks and 6–12 months — not ALT. Check ALT only when symptoms suggest hepatotoxicity. Routine CK monitoring is also COR 3 No Benefit (LOE A). Clinical thresholds: ALT >3× ULN with symptoms and CK >10× ULN with symptoms warrant discontinuation (FDA labeling). See [statin-intolerance] for the symptomatic-rechallenge pathway.

faqs.title: Severely elevated LDL — workup and management
faqs.first_layer_html:
Initiate high-intensity statin at the visit LDL ≥190 is confirmed, regardless of risk score (COR 1).[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026] A confirmatory repeat lipid panel before starting is reasonable practice but not required — do not delay statin initiation while awaiting confirmation.

Concurrently:

  • Exclude secondary causes (Table 15): hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, obstructive/cholestatic liver disease, CKD, ketogenic or very-low-carb diets, glucocorticoids, estrogens, cyclosporine, atypical antipsychotics, high-dose thiazides, androgens, menopause (NLA 2026)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:nla-fh-2026]. Order TSH, urine protein-creatinine, hepatic panel, and a dietary/medication history.
  • Evaluate for FH — see [fh-management].

sub_questions.question: Should I initiate combination therapy upfront for severe hyperchol + ASCVD?
sub_questions.answer_html: For severe hypercholesterolemia + ASCVD specifically: yes — the 2026 guideline's "and/or" language for nonstatin add-ons supports upfront combination at the first visit, and these patients "almost always require aggressive combination therapy."[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026] For typical (non-severe-hyperchol) ASCVD patients, the 2026 guideline does not explicitly call for upfront combination as COR 1 — secondary-prevention recommendations still reference maximally tolerated statin as the prerequisite before adding nonstatins[ref:bergmark-lancet-2022].

faqs.title: Familial hypercholesterolemia — diagnosis, genetic testing, cascade, pediatric
faqs.first_layer_html: Suspect FH in any adult with LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL after secondary causes are excluded. The 2026 ACC/AHA guideline emphasizes genetic testing as the primary diagnostic approach — three clinical scoring systems exist (Dutch Lipid Clinic Network, Simon Broome, MEDPED) as adjuncts when genetic testing is unavailable, but no single framework is formally endorsed as primary[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. Physical findings (tendinous xanthomata, corneal arcus before age 45) are highly specific but not sensitive — absence does not rule out FH.[ref:singh-jacc-2019][ref:qureshi-cochrane-2021]

sub_questions.question: When is genetic testing indicated?
sub_questions.answer_html:
The 2026 ACC/AHA stratifies genetic testing by FH suspicion:

  • COR 1 (LOE B-NR): adults with possible/probable/definite clinical FH — significant upgrade from prior guidelines[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:sturm-jacc-2018]
  • COR 2a (LOE B-NR): LDL-C ≥190 mg/dL without identifiable secondary cause
  • COR 2b (LOE B-NR): LDL-C 160–189 mg/dL without secondary cause

The 4-gene FH panel covers LDLR, APOB, PCSK9, LDLRAP1. Clinically definite cases lack an identifiable pathogenic variant in ~20–40% — a negative gene panel does not rule out FH[ref:schunkert-nejm-2026]; clinical management proceeds on the same pathway.

sub_questions.question: How do I approach cascade screening?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Cascade lipid screening for first- and second-degree relatives of patients with premature ASCVD, severe hypercholesterolemia, or FH is COR 2a (a downgrade from earlier COR 1 framings[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]). Operationally: index patient → first-degree relatives age ≥2 → extend to second-degree if positives identified. PCP-initiated cascade conversations are appropriate clinical practice.

FH and elevated Lp(a) are independent inherited risk factors[ref:trinder-jacc-2020][ref:ellis-jacc-2019] — FH does not cause elevated Lp(a). Both can co-occur in the same family. Order Lp(a) per the universal COR 1 once-in-lifetime recommendation regardless of FH status.

sub_questions.question: What about pediatric FH — when to screen and start a statin?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Universal pediatric lipid screening: age 9–11 (COR 1, LOE B-NR)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. The "second screening at 17–21" comes from the 2011 NHLBI Expert Panel / AAP endorsement — not from the 2026 ACC/AHA guideline. Cascade screening from age 2 is supported in known-FH families[ref:gidding-circ-2015].

For children with HeFH: statin can be initiated at age 8–10, targeting LDL-C <130 mg/dL or ≥50% reduction[ref:gidding-circ-2015][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. Specialty (pediatric lipid) involvement is recommended for HoFH, where lomitapide, evinacumab, or lipoprotein apheresis may be indicated[ref:raal-atherosclerosis-2018].

sub_questions.question: What's the counseling frame for FH?
sub_questions.answer_html: FH is a lifelong condition with cumulative LDL-C burden driving CV risk[ref:schunkert-nejm-2026][ref:nla-fh-2026]. Management is a multi-decade plan: aggressive LDL-C reduction from the FH-confirmation visit (or childhood when diagnosed early), tight monitoring, and family counseling. The benefit-risk equation strongly favors continued statin therapy across the lifespan — ASCVD prevention benefit far outweighs statin-induced T2D risk per COR 1 in this population (see [statin-T2D]).

faqs.title: Escalation when LDL-C or non-HDL-C is not at goal
faqs.first_layer_html:
Step 1: Confirm adherence and titrate to maximally tolerated statin (preferred: atorvastatin or rosuvastatin).[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]

Step 2: Add a nonstatin agent. The 2026 guideline removes the requirement that ezetimibe must precede a PCSK9 mAb — choice may now be based on degree of LDL-C lowering needed and patient preference.[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]

Escalation trigger: failure to achieve the tier-specific goal. VHR uses LDL-C <55 as the trigger; non-VHR ASCVD uses <70 (with COR 2a option to intensify to <55). A VHR patient at LDL-C 60 on max statin is already a candidate for nonstatin add-on.

sub_questions.question: What's the PA and coverage reality for nonstatin agents?
sub_questions.answer_html:
PCSK9 mAbs and inclisiran require PA on commercial and Medicare. Typical PA gates: documented maximally tolerated statin + LDL-C above threshold (usually ≥70 mg/dL for ASCVD, ≥100 for FH); ezetimibe trial often required even though the 2026 guideline no longer mandates it clinically. "Maximally tolerated statin therapy" is broader than "statin intolerance or failure"[ref:acc-2022-decisionpathway][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026] — use the former in PA language.

Bempedoic acid generally requires PA. DDI alert: bempedoic acid + simvastatin >20 mg/day or pravastatin 40 mg/day → ~2-fold increase in statin plasma levels[ref:fda-nexletol-2026][ref:aha-acc-ccd-2023]. Switch to atorvastatin or rosuvastatin before adding bempedoic acid, or use ezetimibe instead.

faqs.title: IPE, bempedoic acid, inclisiran — when each fits
faqs.first_layer_html: This entry provides decision support for the three nonstatin add-ons with nuanced placement. For the LDL-lowering escalation pathway (ezetimibe / PCSK9 mAb / bempedoic acid / inclisiran), see [not-at-goal].

sub_questions.question: When is icosapent ethyl (IPE) appropriate?
sub_questions.answer_html:
IPE (high-purity EPA, 2 g BID) is COR 2b for adults ≥50 with ASCVD or DM + ≥1 additional risk factor, on statin with managed LDL-C goal, and TG 150–499 mg/dL[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026].

REDUCE-IT showed 25% RRR MACE[ref:reduce-it-2019][ref:bhatt-jacc-2019], with benefit visible across all baseline TG tertiles (including TG <200). The COR 2b — rather than COR 2a — reflects the mineral-oil placebo controversy: biomarker analysis suggests the placebo arm experienced deleterious changes, likely exaggerating the observed effect[ref:dixon-amjmed-2020]. STRENGTH (mixed EPA/DHA, corn-oil placebo) was negative[ref:goldberg-dca-2020] for the same indication. OTC omega-3/fish oil products are not equivalent and are not recommended for CV risk reduction.

Use the 2026 TG ≥150 mg/dL threshold for IPE, not the REDUCE-IT enrollment cutoff of 135 mg/dL[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026].

sub_questions.question: Bempedoic acid — where does it fit?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Bempedoic acid is COR 2a as a general add-on to statin and/or ezetimibe and/or PCSK9 mAb in patients not at LDL-C goal[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. The FDA label has two distinct indications:

  • LDL-C reduction in primary hyperlipidemia including HeFH — broad adjunctive scope, not restricted to statin-intolerant
  • CV risk reduction in adults unable to take recommended statin therapy — limited to statin-intolerant per CLEAR Outcomes enrollment[ref:fda-nexletol-2026][ref:clear-outcomes-2023]

These diverge: payers may follow the FDA CV-risk-reduction indication (statin-intolerant only) for PA even though the ACC/AHA recommends broader use.

sub_questions.question: When does inclisiran fit better than a PCSK9 mAb?
sub_questions.answer_html: Reserve inclisiran for patients who: cannot tolerate evolocumab or alirocumab; cannot access them (insurance/pharmacy); show poor adherence to self-injected PCSK9 mAbs; or strongly prefer twice-yearly dosing. Inclisiran is administered in-office (Medicare Part B buy-and-bill) — simpler access than PCSK9 mAbs (Part D, self-administered)[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. PA framing: inclisiran's FDA indication is hypercholesterolemia broadly (including HeFH), not ASCVD-specific — payers gating on ASCVD-specific FDA indication may deny[ref:mulligan-jcl-2026].

faqs.first_layer_html:
CAC scoring is COR 1 (LOE B-NR) for risk reclassification in intermediate-risk and select borderline-risk adults — upgraded from COR 2a in the 2018 guideline[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]. Eligible: men ≥40, women ≥45.

sub_questions.question: What does the benefit-risk discussion cover?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Per the AHA Statin Safety Scientific Statement and CTT Collaboration meta-analyses[ref:newman-atvb-2019][ref:ctt-collaboration-2012][ref:collins-lancet-2016][ref:silverman-jama-2016]:

  • Benefit: ~21% proportional reduction in major vascular events per 1 mmol/L (~38.7 mg/dL) LDL-C reduction (24% after the first year). CTT 2012: 11 fewer major vascular events per 1,000 treated over 5 years per 1 mmol/L reduction in low-risk populations[ref:ctt-collaboration-2012][ref:silverman-jama-2016].
  • Safety: No causal association with cancer, dementia, cognitive impairment, or hemorrhagic stroke. True statin myopathy: 1–10 per 10,000 person-years; rhabdomyolysis: 1–3 per 100,000[ref:newman-atvb-2019].
  • Statin-induced T2D: real but small — see [statin-T2D].

For MCI patients and families: FOURIER prespecified secondary, EBBINGHAUS, and the Sabatine 2018 JAMA Cardiology meta-analysis of IMPROVE-IT/FOURIER/REVEAL all show no neurocognitive harm[ref:giugliano-lancet-2017][ref:rosenson-jacc-2018][ref:sabatine-jamacardio-2018] at very low achieved LDL-C.

faqs.title: Identifying intolerance, nocebo, and rechallenge
faqs.first_layer_html:
The nocebo effect accounts for most statin-attributed symptoms. SAMSON (Howard et al. JACC 2021) showed ~90% of statin-attributed symptoms were nocebo-driven in a crossover design[ref:samson-jacc-2021]: mean symptom scores 16.3 statin / 15.4 placebo / 8.0 no tablet (P=0.388 statin vs placebo). 50% of participants successfully restarted statin therapy after the trial.

Generalizability caveat: the NLA Clinical Perspective on SAMS (Warden 2023) notes SAMSON and StatinWISE results cannot be generalized to all patients given the small, self-selected enrolled populations[ref:warden-jcl-2023]. Use nocebo data to guide rechallenge counseling, not to dismiss patient experience.

sub_questions.question: What is the rechallenge protocol?
sub_questions.answer_html:
The 2022 ACC ECDP recommends at least 2 (preferably 3) statins, including at least 1 attempt at the lowest approved daily dose or alternative dosing, before declaring intolerance.[ref:acc-2022-decisionpathway] The 2026 ACC/AHA does not specify a numeric trial count[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026] — the "≥2 (preferably 3) trials" framing belongs to the 2022 ECDP, not 2026.

Rechallenge tactics:

  • Start low-dose atorvastatin or rosuvastatin (preferred agents)
  • Try every-other-day or 3×/week dosing — long half-lives support intermittent dosing
  • Pause 2–4 weeks, then rechallenge — symptom attribution often shifts on the second pass[ref:warden-jcl-2023][ref:newman-atvb-2019]
  • If true myopathy is suspected: check CK. CK >10× ULN with symptoms warrants discontinuation (FDA labeling).
  • If two-statin failure is genuine: bempedoic acid (FDA CV-risk indication in statin-intolerant) and ezetimibe become first-line LDL-C–lowering options.

faqs.title: Statin-induced T2D, intensity dependence, and FH cohort
faqs.first_layer_html:
Statin-induced T2D is real but should not drive discontinuation or down-titration. The ASCVD prevention benefit clearly outweighs T2D risk per COR 1 in 2026[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. Continue statin in patients who develop T2D on therapy.

The CTT Collaboration 2024 individual-patient-data meta-analysis found an intensity-dependent effect[ref:ctt-collaboration-2024]:

  • Moderate-intensity: RR 1.10 (10% relative risk increase)
  • High-intensity: RR 1.36 (36% relative risk increase)

The earlier "9–12% RRI" intensity-flat figure is not supported. 62% of new-onset T2D diagnoses occur in patients already in the top quartile of baseline glycemia — most diagnoses are accelerated, not created[ref:ctt-collaboration-2024].

sub_questions.question: Does this T2D risk apply differently to FH patients?
sub_questions.answer_html: FH-specific cohort data on statin-induced T2D are not robustly available in the retrieved literature (EAS-FHSC, SAFEHEART, or CASCADE FH registries). The 2026 ACC/AHA does not provide FH-specific guidance.[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026] The general principle holds: ASCVD prevention benefit far outweighs T2D risk in HeFH given lifelong elevated LDL-C burden[ref:nla-fh-2026]. Do not reduce statin intensity in FH patients due to T2D risk; monitor HbA1c/fasting glucose per standard. Counsel without minimizing — the risk is real but small relative to FH-driven CV risk.

faqs.title: Statin therapy in pregnancy vs lactation
faqs.first_layer_html:
Pregnancy and lactation require different assessments — do not conflate the two.

  • Pregnancy: The July 2021 FDA labeling update removed the blanket contraindication for most statins. For VHR ASCVD or FH patients with additional risk factors, statin therapy "may be considered" per the 2026 ACC/AHA[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. For most pregnant patients, "it seems prudent to avoid statin therapy." Individualized benefit-risk discussion per the 2022 ACC ECDP and 2024 NLA Consensus on dyslipidemia in women of reproductive potential[ref:acc-2022-decisionpathway][ref:agarwala-jcl-2024].
  • Lactation: The contraindication remains in place per FDA labeling. The 2021 FDA change applied to pregnancy only.[ref:kovacic-circ-2026] Do not restart or initiate statins in patients who are breastfeeding.

faqs.title: Identifying and managing VHR patients
faqs.first_layer_html: VHR reclassification changes the LDL-C goal from <70 to <55 mg/dL and the non-HDL-C goal from <100 to <85 mg/dL[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026]. See [ldl-target] for the full VHR criteria (≥2 major ASCVD events, or 1 major ASCVD event + ≥2 high-risk conditions)[ref:acc-2022-decisionpathway][ref:aha-acc-ccd-2023].

sub_questions.question: Does VHR reclassification require cardiology referral?
sub_questions.answer_html: Not automatically. PCPs can manage VHR patients on maximally tolerated statin + ezetimibe + bempedoic acid (where appropriate) within scope. Refer to cardiology when LDL-C remains >55 mg/dL despite max statin + ezetimibe and PCSK9 mAb initiation is being considered, or when the patient has complex/recent ACS[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-2022-decisionpathway], advanced HF, or device-related issues. The consult builder for cardiology is in the spawn menu.

faqs.title: Lp(a) and ApoB — ordering and interpretation
faqs.first_layer_html:
Lp(a): COR 1 once-in-lifetime in all adults. Order with the next routine lipid draw if not yet measured; document in the lifetime problem list. Key thresholds[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc]: ≥125 nmol/L (≥50 mg/dL) = elevated; ≥250 nmol/L (≥100 mg/dL) = ≥2-fold CV risk.

ApoB: COR 2a on LLT for residual-risk evaluation — most useful in patients with ASCVD, CKM syndrome, T2D, or TG ≥150 mg/dL once LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals are near target.[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:fegers-wustrow-jacc-2022]

Full framework for both markers is in [co-primary-targets].

sub_questions.question: Are ApoB and Lp(a) covered by insurance?
sub_questions.answer_html: Both are covered by most commercial and Medicare plans without prior authorization. Some plans require a diagnosis code for Lp(a) (e.g., E78.5 mixed hyperlipidemia; Z83.42 family history of lipid disorder). Out-of-pocket when uncovered: ~$20–60 ApoB / ~$30–80 Lp(a). Neither is auto-included in routine lipid panels — order specifically. Both can be embedded in Epic order sets / SmartSets.

faqs.title: What changed since the 2018 cholesterol guideline
faqs.first_layer_html:
Five changes with direct clinical impact in the 2026 ACC/AHA Multisociety Dyslipidemia Guideline:

  • PREVENT replaces PCE as the primary risk estimator — recalibrated tiers (Low <3% / Borderline 3–<5% / Intermediate 5–<10% / High ≥10%), extended age range 30–79, and new 30-year risk pathway for younger adults[ref:khan-circ-2024][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:krishnan-jacc-2025].
  • LDL-C and non-HDL-C are co-primary treatment targets — reinstated explicit numeric goals across all tiers, departing from 2018 percentage-reduction-only framing[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:abbasi-jama-2026][ref:grundy-2018-cholesterol].
  • Lp(a) is COR 1 once-in-lifetime universal screening — upgraded from risk enhancer in selected populations[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:acc-aha-dys-2026-jacc].
  • Escalation sequencing is no longer rigid — ezetimibe no longer required before PCSK9 mAb; bempedoic acid and inclisiran now named agents in the toolkit[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:clear-outcomes-2023].
  • Icosapent ethyl (IPE) is COR 2b for residual TG-driven risk — adults ≥50 with ASCVD/DM on statin with TG 150–499 mg/dL[ref:acc-aha-dys-2026][ref:reduce-it-2019]. OTC fish oil not equivalent.

sub_questions.question: Will VHR vs non-VHR collapse in the next guideline?
sub_questions.answer_html: The 2026 writing committee has signaled that future revisions may collapse VHR vs non-VHR ASCVD into a single LDL-C <55 mg/dL pathway for all ASCVD patients, pending VESALIUS-CV trial results[ref:blumenthal-circ-2026-progress]. The 2026 COR 2a option to intensify non-VHR ASCVD to <55 is an early step. Module structure stays VHR-vs-non-VHR for now; expect this to consolidate in the next ACC/AHA dyslipidemia revision.

modules.landing_intro: A patient has an abnormal creatinine, or you've ordered cystatin C and the eGFR came back lower than expected. Use this checklist to complete a reasonable initial workup before escalating. Nephrology should receive a patient you've already started working — not one you're handing off cold.

Establish baseline: order cystatin C if not yet done, BMP, CBC, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR), urinalysis with microscopy
Stage the CKD using cystatin C-based eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021) and albuminuria category — document G and A stage
Blood pressure at goal for CKD (< 120/80 if tolerated) — document current readings and agent

green_zone.zone_label: All boxes checked — You've done the work

modules.escalation_section_label: Escalate to nephrology consult if any apply

escalation.statement: eGFR decline > 5 mL/min/1.73m² in 12 months, or > 10 in 24 months
eGFR < 30 (G4–G5) at any point
uACR > 300 mg/g (severely increased albuminuria)
Unexplained CKD — no clear etiology after initial workup (no diabetes, no hypertension, no obstructive history)
Persistent hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs on microscopy

faqs.title: Nephrotoxins and dose-adjusted drugs — what to look for

items.question: What medications should I flag immediately?
items.answer_html:
High-priority nephrotoxins to review in any CKD patient:

NSAIDs (including OTC ibuprofen/naproxen) — counsel to discontinue.

Metformin — generally safe to eGFR 30, reduce monitoring frequency below 45, hold below 30.

SGLT2 inhibitors — reassess below eGFR 45 (varies by agent and indication).

ACE inhibitors / ARBs — do not discontinue for mild creatinine bump (up to 30% rise is acceptable and expected); do reassess if rise exceeds that threshold.

Gabapentin/pregabalin — dose reduction required below eGFR 60.

Renally-cleared antibiotics — flag for any acute prescribing: nitrofurantoin contraindicated below eGFR 45.

items.question: My patient is on an NSAID for chronic pain. Do I stop it today?
items.answer_html:
In CKD G3a and above (eGFR < 60), the recommendation is to discontinue chronic NSAID use. Have a direct conversation: frame it as protecting kidney function, not removing pain management.

Offer alternatives — acetaminophen, topical diclofenac for localized pain, or a warm handoff to pain management if the underlying condition warrants it. Document the conversation and the plan.

items.question: Should I adjust doses myself or wait for nephrology?
items.answer_html:
For common medications with well-established renal dosing (metformin, gabapentin, many antibiotics), adjust now using the eGFR-based thresholds above. Do not wait for nephrology to make changes that are your responsibility as the PCP.

The consult is for guidance on management strategy — not for permission to stop nephrotoxins.

faqs.title: What to order and why — the CKD baseline panel

items.question: Why cystatin C if I already have a creatinine-based eGFR?
items.answer_html:
Creatinine-based eGFR is affected by muscle mass, diet, and race — it systematically overestimates GFR in patients with low muscle mass (elderly, frail, malnourished) and can underestimate in bodybuilders.

Cystatin C is filtered at a constant rate regardless of these variables. The CKD-EPI 2021 equation using both markers is now the preferred standard. When cystatin C eGFR is meaningfully lower than creatinine eGFR, believe cystatin C — it's the more accurate number.

items.question: My patient's cystatin C eGFR came back 15 points lower than their creatinine eGFR. Is that real?
items.answer_html:
Often yes. This is the most common anxiety point with cystatin C adoption. The lower number is not an error — it's a more accurate reflection of true GFR, particularly in older or leaner patients.

Stage and manage based on the cystatin C result. If this moves the patient into a higher-risk category, that's exactly the information you needed.

items.question: What does the uACR add?
items.answer_html:
Albuminuria is an independent risk factor for CKD progression and cardiovascular disease, separate from eGFR. A patient can have eGFR 65 with uACR > 300 and be at higher risk than a patient with eGFR 52 and uACR < 30.

Staging requires both dimensions — the G stage (eGFR) and the A stage (albuminuria). You cannot complete a CKD staging without it.

items.question: Does the urinalysis with microscopy need to be a fresh catch?
items.answer_html:
Ideally yes — a fresh midstream catch within 2 hours of collection gives the most reliable microscopy, particularly for RBC morphology. If the patient is in office, collect it that day.

If ordering remotely, instruct accordingly and note in the order.

faqs.title: Staging with cystatin C eGFR — what the numbers mean

items.question: What are the GFR stages and what do they mean clinically?
items.answer_html:
Using CKD-EPI 2021 cystatin C-based eGFR:

G1: ≥ 90 — Normal or high. CKD diagnosis requires other markers (albuminuria, structural abnormality). Monitor.

G2: 60–89 — Mildly decreased. Monitor annually if stable.

G3a: 45–59 — Mildly to moderately decreased. Begin medication review, BP optimization, RAAS therapy if proteinuric.

G3b: 30–44 — Moderately to severely decreased. Nephrology consult appropriate. Begin anemia workup, mineral/bone disease labs.

G4: 15–29 — Severely decreased. Nephrology referral (not just consult). RRT planning discussion begins.

G5: < 15 — Kidney failure. Active nephrology co-management required.

items.question: My patient is G3a. What do I actually do at this visit?
items.answer_html:
Three things: (1) Start or optimize an ACE inhibitor or ARB if they have albuminuria or diabetes — this is the single highest-impact intervention in early CKD. (2) Get BP below 120/80 if tolerated. (3) Counsel on nephrotoxin avoidance and dietary sodium restriction.

An SGLT2 inhibitor is indicated if they have diabetes or heart failure — this is now a standard of care intervention, not a specialist decision.

items.question: Do I need to tell the patient they have CKD?
items.answer_html:
Yes — this is a diagnosis, and it should be documented and communicated as such. Many patients with CKD G3 have been managed for years without anyone saying the words. Naming it clearly allows the patient to understand the stakes, engage in self-management, and make informed decisions.

Use plain language: "Your kidneys are working at about X% of normal. This is a condition called chronic kidney disease. It's manageable and we caught it at a stage where we can do a lot to protect them."

faqs.title: BP targets in CKD — tighter than you might think

items.question: Is 130/80 good enough?
items.answer_html:
Current KDIGO 2021 guidelines recommend a target of < 120 mmHg systolic if tolerated, based on SPRINT trial data. This is a meaningful shift from the older 130/80 standard.

In practice, tolerability is the limiting factor — orthostatic symptoms, syncope risk in elderly patients, and baseline hypotension all require individualization. Document your target and your rationale.

items.question: Which agents are preferred?
items.answer_html:
ACE inhibitor or ARB is first-line in CKD with albuminuria (uACR > 30) or diabetes, regardless of BP. Do not use both together — dual RAAS blockade increases harm without added benefit.

For additional BP control: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone preferred over HCTZ in CKD) are appropriate add-ons. Loop diuretics for volume management in G4–G5.

items.question: My patient's creatinine bumped after I started the ACE inhibitor. Should I stop it?
items.answer_html:
Not automatically. A rise in creatinine of up to 30% after initiating an ACE inhibitor or ARB is expected, acceptable, and does not indicate harm — it reflects the intended hemodynamic effect on the glomerulus.

Recheck in 2 weeks. If the rise is greater than 30% or potassium rises above 5.5, then hold and reassess. If you stop every ACE inhibitor that causes any creatinine bump, you will deprive CKD patients of their most protective therapy.

faqs.title: eGFR declining faster than expected — what to do

items.question: How do I know if the decline is rapid?
items.answer_html:
Pull prior creatinine values from the chart — at minimum 12 months back, ideally 24. Calculate the trajectory. A decline of more than 5 mL/min/1.73m² per year is considered rapid and warrants consult regardless of current stage.

A single low value without prior data is not the same as demonstrated progression — establish the trend first.

items.question: Could something acute be driving this?
items.answer_html:
Yes — always rule out AKI superimposed on CKD before concluding progression. Recent illness, volume depletion, new nephrotoxin exposure, or urinary obstruction can all cause acute drops.

If there's any question, recheck in 4–6 weeks after addressing potential acute factors before framing as progression.

faqs.title: eGFR < 30 — escalation and preparation

items.question: What changes at G4?
items.answer_html:
Several things happen simultaneously at G4 that go beyond standard PCP management:

(1) Nephrology referral (not just consult) is indicated. (2) Mineral and bone disease workup: PTH, phosphorus, 25-OH vitamin D, calcium. (3) Anemia of CKD evaluation. (4) RRT planning conversation — not to alarm, but to inform. Patients who arrive at dialysis having never discussed it are poorly prepared.

items.question: Should I be starting erythropoiesis-stimulating agents?
items.answer_html:
ESA initiation in CKD is a nephrology decision. Your role at G4 is to identify anemia, complete the workup (iron studies, B12, folate, retic count), correct iron deficiency if present, and document.

The consult to nephrology should include this workup so they can advise on ESA candidacy with full information in hand.

faqs.title: Severely increased albuminuria — uACR > 300

items.question: Is this nephrotic range?
items.answer_html:
Not necessarily — nephrotic range proteinuria is traditionally defined as > 3.5 g/day on 24-hour urine, or roughly uACR > 2000–3500 mg/g. A uACR of 300–2000 is severely increased but not nephrotic.

However, any uACR > 300 warrants consult regardless of eGFR, as it indicates significant glomerular pathology and accelerated progression risk.

items.question: Should I repeat it before acting?
items.answer_html:
A single elevated uACR should be confirmed on a second sample (ideally first morning void) before staging — transient elevations occur with fever, exercise, and UTI.

However, if the value is markedly elevated (> 300) and there's no obvious transient cause, begin the workup in parallel with confirmation rather than waiting.

faqs.title: CKD without a clear cause

items.question: My patient has CKD but no diabetes, no hypertension, no obstructive history. What now?
items.answer_html:
This is the consult indication — unexplained CKD requires nephrology input to consider glomerulonephritis, genetic nephropathy, or other primary renal disease.

Before the consult, complete: urinalysis with microscopy (looking for casts), uACR, renal ultrasound, serum protein electrophoresis in patients > 40 (to screen for myeloma), ANA and complement if clinical picture suggests autoimmune.

Document what you've ruled out — the nephrologist can then focus on what remains.

faqs.title: Persistent hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs

items.question: What do dysmorphic RBCs mean?
items.answer_html:
Dysmorphic RBCs — particularly acanthocytes — on urine microscopy indicate glomerular origin of bleeding, as opposed to urothelial sources (stone, tumor, infection). This is a nephrology finding, not a urology finding.

If the microscopy report specifically mentions dysmorphic RBCs or acanthocytes, the consult goes to nephrology, not to urology for cystoscopy.

items.question: What if the report just says "RBCs present" without commenting on morphology?
items.answer_html:
Standard urinalysis does not assess morphology — that requires microscopy with a trained eye. If you have > 5 RBCs/hpf on two separate specimens without an obvious benign cause, request formal microscopy.

In many practices this requires a specific order or a call to the lab.

consults.label: Psychiatry consult
consults.blurb: General psychiatry — diagnostic uncertainty, ceiling-dose escalation, mood/anxiety comorbidity.

decision_tree.question: Does the patient have a documented co-occurring substance use disorder (SUD) or active substance misuse?
decision_tree.hint: Per ASAM/AAAP 2024, stimulant prescribing in patients with SUD is supported but ideally co-managed with addiction-medicine expertise. If yes, addiction psychiatry is the better-matched consult.

decision_tree.question: Has the patient required dose escalation past the FDA ceiling without a documented rationale, or are escalation requests recent and rapid?
decision_tree.hint: Continuing a maximum-dose prescription is within PCP scope when justified and documented. Without documented rationale, an external review supports the prescribing decision.

decision_tree.question: Are there other red flags — diagnostic uncertainty, comorbid mood/anxiety not responding, behavioral inconsistency on PDMP, or safety concerns?
decision_tree.hint: Comorbid PTSD, treatment-resistant anxiety/mood, or unexplained PDMP patterns benefit from psychiatric input — both for clinical management and for documentation.
decision_tree.block_text: No clear consult indication today. Continue PCP management with documented rationale; reassess at the next visit. Pull this builder back up if a red flag emerges.

faqs.title: What counts as a concerning pattern?
faqs.first_layer_html:
How often must I check the PDMP?

StateRequired frequency
New York (I-STOP)Before every prescription event — no exceptions for stable patients[ref:ny-pbh-3343a]
New JerseyAt first prescription, then quarterly during ongoing therapy[ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1]
Other statesVerify with your compliance office — requirements vary

Best practice in both states: check at every renewal visit regardless of statutory minimum.

Patterns that warrant a closer look

  • Overlapping prescribers without documented coordination
  • Multiple pharmacies (≥4) without a clear reason — insurance, shortage, or geography often explain this
  • Concurrent opioid prescription — clarify the indication; don't reflexively discontinue
  • Dose-quantity discrepancy across dispensing records

Reassuring pattern: same prescriber, same pharmacy, consistent quantity, no overlapping controlled-substance prescriptions.

sub_questions.question: The prior provider didn't document any PDMP checks. Am I starting over?
sub_questions.answer_html: Yes — when you become prescriber of record, the documentation obligation transfers to you. The prior provider's omission is their liability, not yours, but your first check is essential before issuing your first prescription. Think of it as a brief triage at the handoff appointment — under two minutes, and your best protection.

sub_questions.question: I see something concerning. What do I do?
sub_questions.answer_html: Do not prescribe at this visit. Have a direct, non-accusatory conversation: "I'm seeing some things in the prescription history I want to understand before we go further." Document exactly what you found and what the patient told you. If the concern is significant, this is an appropriate trigger for a psychiatry consult — the specific question being a safe prescribing plan, not routine review.

faqs.smartphrase_note: PDMP concern documented — consider .CSADHD-PDMP-HOLD (future)

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: PDMP review prior to stimulant renewal revealed [finding]. Requesting guidance on safe prescribing plan.

faqs.title: What if there's a substance use disorder in the history?
faqs.first_layer_html:
A past or active SUD is a risk factor requiring enhanced monitoring — not an automatic disqualifier. ASAM/AAAP (2024) explicitly supports stimulant therapy in patients with co-occurring ADHD and SUD when benefits outweigh risks.[ref:asam-aaap-2024] Stimulant treatment in this population is associated with fewer hospitalizations, lower suicidal ideation rates, and reduced mortality.[ref:baweja-jaacap-2025]

Recommended monitoring when SUD is present

  • Prefer extended-release or prodrug formulations (Vyvanse, Adderall XR, Concerta) over IR
  • PDMP review at state-required cadence (see PDMP topic)
  • Urine drug screening — discuss expectations up front; not punitive
  • Pill counts at random intervals + increased visit frequency
  • Document awareness of SUD history and monitoring plan — SmartPhrase: .CSADHD-SUD-AWARE
Guideline tension: AAFP 2024 lists active drug addiction among contraindications;[ref:aafp-2024] ASAM/AAAP 2024 treats it as a risk factor requiring monitoring.[ref:asam-aaap-2024] Document which framework you're working from.

sub_questions.question: The patient currently uses cannabis. Does that count?
sub_questions.answer_html: The clinically relevant distinction is between cannabis use and cannabis use disorder (CUD). Mere use is common and generally non-actionable.[ref:ryan-jad-2025] CUD is clinically actionable: patients with CUD show substantially reduced response to ADHD pharmacotherapy (OR 0.20–0.24).[ref:carbone-jcm-2026] When CUD is present, expect attenuated treatment effect, address CUD as a co-occurring disorder, and apply the SUD monitoring framework. Occasional recreational use in a stable, functional patient is a documentation point, not an escalation trigger.

sub_questions.question: The patient is on buprenorphine for OUD and also takes a stimulant. Is that high-risk?
sub_questions.answer_html: Not necessarily — and the data run counter to intuition. A recent Canadian cohort found prescribed stimulants combined with buprenorphine were associated with reduced overdose risk (aHR 0.47).[ref:young-bc-addiction-2025] Concurrent stimulant + opioid without a documented pain rationale warrants clarification, but do not reflexively discontinue. Confirm the indication and document your reasoning.

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Patient with co-occurring ADHD and [active / recent] SUD; requesting addiction-medicine input on monitoring plan and formulation choice. Continuation otherwise within PCP scope.

faqs.smartphrase_note: .CSADHD-SUD-AWARE — Continuation with active or past SUD history — enhanced monitoring plan in place per ASAM/AAAP 2024 framework (future)

faqs.title: How do I assess whether the medication is actually working?
faqs.first_layer_html:
You are not re-validating the original diagnosis from scratch. You are verifying that the inherited prescription is delivering documented function and that the prescribing context is safe.

Practical assessment at the inheritance visit

  • Review available records — prior ADHD evaluation, school history, prior ratings
  • Ask directly: "What did the medication change for you, and what would change if you stopped?"
  • Screen for misuse — PDMP, fill patterns, brief substance-use screen
  • Specific, credible functional improvements are a reasonable basis for continuation

Brief structured symptom and function assessment at each renewal is recommended. Formal rating scales (ASRS, Conners) are not required at every visit — no US guideline mandates this.[ref:aafp-2024]

sub_questions.question: The patient says it's working but I'm not sure I believe them.
sub_questions.answer_html: Look for corroboration: prior notes from a previous provider, a therapist, a partner or employer, or a prior rating scale.[ref:marshall-clinneuropsych-2021] Check for behavioral inconsistencies — does the PDMP pattern, presentation, or history suggest misuse rather than treatment?[ref:cepeda-ajdaa-2015] If your clinical instinct is firing and you can't articulate why you're comfortable, pause, document, and consider a consult. That consult is not punitive — it's the framework doing its job.

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Patient on inherited stimulant prescription requesting continuation. Provider uncertainty regarding efficacy and diagnostic basis. Please evaluate and advise.

faqs.title: Early fill requests — what's the threshold?
faqs.first_layer_html:
Note: The "5-day early" threshold and "2+ early fills in 12 months" pattern are PBM/pharmacy dispensing conventions — not clinical guideline thresholds. No CDC, SAMHSA, ASAM, AAFP, FDA, or DEA guidance specifies a numeric early-fill cutoff for stimulants.

A single early fill is worth documenting and may warrant a brief conversation. A repeated pattern warrants individualized clinical-risk assessment, PDMP review, and consideration of a urine drug screen. Context matters — vacation timing, the 2022–2024 stimulant shortage, and partial-fill days-supply confusion all generate early-fill appearances that are clinically benign.

sub_questions.question: Can I fill early for travel or vacation?
sub_questions.answer_html: Yes — federal law (21 CFR §1306.12) explicitly permits issuing multiple sequential prescriptions totaling up to 90 days of supply, with an "earliest fill date" noted on each.[ref:cfr-1306-12] The early-fill barrier patients encounter is usually a PBM days-supply edit, not a legal prohibition. State law may add restrictions — verify with your compliance office before issuing post-dated Schedule II prescriptions.

sub_questions.question: The patient says they lost the medication. What do I do?
sub_questions.answer_html: Federal law does not categorically prohibit issuing a new prescription for a lost Schedule II medication — validity is governed by "legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of practice."[ref:cfr-1306-04] Most institutions adopt a no-replacement policy as a risk-management standard; that is institutional policy, not federal regulation. Communicate this honestly: "Our practice doesn't replace lost Schedule II prescriptions as a matter of policy — the DEA framework allows clinical discretion, but our institutional standard is no replacement." Document the report, check the PDMP, note the conversation. A single loss event is not disqualifying; a pattern warrants escalation.

faqs.smartphrase_note: Early fill pattern documented — consider .CSADHD-EARLYFILL-DISCUSS (future)

faqs.title: The prior diagnosis looks thin. Now what?
faqs.first_layer_html:
You are not responsible for the prior diagnostic process. You are responsible for decisions made from this point forward. The question is not "was this diagnosis legitimate?" — it's "do I have enough information to comfortably continue this medication?"

A reasonable adult workup should have included

  • Validated rating scale (ASRS or comparable)
  • Structured clinical interview — symptom onset before age 12, cross-setting impairment
  • Collateral information — school records, prior evaluations, observer report (self-report alone has poor specificity)[ref:cepeda-ajdaa-2015]
  • Differential and comorbidity screen — anxiety, mood disorders, SUD, sleep disorders, thyroid

If none of this is in the chart, use the consult pathway — not to penalize the patient, but to get expert documentation in the record. It changes the risk profile for both of you.

sub_questions.question: Is neuropsychological testing required?
sub_questions.answer_html: No — ADHD is a clinical diagnosis. Neuropsych testing has inadequate sensitivity and specificity as a stand-alone tool. AAFP suggests considering it when collateral information is lacking, malingering is suspected, or significant psychiatric comorbidity is present.[ref:aafp-2024] Combined with a validated rating scale, cognitive testing improves specificity — but it's not a prerequisite.

sub_questions.question: The patient is stable, functional, and has been on this medication for 5 years. Does the thin chart still matter?
sub_questions.answer_html: A long stable course with demonstrated functional benefit is important supporting evidence, but it does not independently validate the diagnosis — stimulants improve focus in many conditions, and roughly 20% of prescription-stimulant misusers exaggerate symptoms.[ref:cepeda-ajdaa-2015] Treat the stable course as supportive, not conclusive. For a primary-care provider, the practical question is "should continuation continue?" — and on that, long-term evidence supports continuing when the patient is stable and functional. A randomized discontinuation study found significant worsening on stopping methylphenidate after 2+ years.[ref:matthijssen-ajp-2019] Document your reasoning. If continuation is uncomfortable, use the consult pathway.

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Patient on inherited stimulant prescription requesting continuation. No formal workup documented in chart. Please evaluate and advise on whether to continue, modify, or obtain formal evaluation.

Doses above the FDA-labeled maximum require specialist co-management. Document explicit clinical rationale for any prescription at or near the ceiling.

sub_questions.question: The patient was escalated to max dose by the prior provider. Do I continue?
sub_questions.answer_html: Continuing a ceiling-dose prescription is within primary care scope if clinically justified and documented. At first visit: review the chart for the escalation rationale. If it's documented and coherent, continue with your own documented review. If there's no rationale — or if the escalation was recent and rapid — this is a consult trigger.

sub_questions.question: What does the dose-response evidence say about going higher?
sub_questions.answer_html: For amphetamines, the symptom-reduction curve plateaus at roughly 30–35 mg/day. Doses above the FDA license offer no detectable additional symptom benefit.[ref:jama-psych-farhat2024] For methylphenidate, doses above 60 mg/day deliver small incremental gains but adverse-event dropout roughly doubles (OR ≈ 2.02). The Concerta ceiling of 72 mg/day is well-calibrated to the evidence curve.
