faqs.title: When function declines despite medication
faqs.first_layer_html:
Behavioral red flags

  • New or worsening irritability, emotional dysregulation, or rage attributed to medication timing
  • Sleep disruption severe enough to impair function, especially if patient is escalating to cope
  • Increasing psychological dependence — inability to function at all without medication, qualitatively beyond therapeutic benefit

If a patient is deteriorating on stimulants, the right move is psychiatric input framed around comorbidity management — what to add, taper, or sequence — not unilateral discontinuation. Name the specific comorbidity concern in the consult.

sub_questions.question: Could this be something other than ADHD at this point?
sub_questions.answer_html: Comorbidity in adult ADHD is the rule, not the exception — ORs of 4.5–8.7 for anxiety, mood, and SUD.[ref:hartman-nbr-2023] The right question is rarely "ADHD or something else?" and is usually "ADHD plus what?" DSM-5-TR distinguishes ADHD by developmental onset and persistence vs. the episodic course of bipolar disorder, the worry-driven cognition of anxiety, and the trauma-linked hypervigilance of PTSD.[ref:dsm-5-tr-2022] If you suspect undiagnosed or undertreated bipolar disorder, stabilize the mood disorder first[ref:viktorin-ajp-2017] — don't simply stop the stimulant.

sub_questions.question: What about anxiety — won't stimulants make it worse?
sub_questions.answer_html: Population-level data run the opposite direction. A meta-analysis of 23 RCTs found stimulants reduced treatment-emergent anxiety (RR 0.86).[ref:coughlin-jcap-2015] Adult safety meta-analyses are consistent — net effect is neutral to favorable. A minority of patients do worsen; stimulants remain first-line even with comorbid anxiety. Monitor, adjust dose if needed, but do not reflexively discontinue.

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Patient on stimulant therapy with [new symptom]. Requesting evaluation for [comorbidity] and guidance on whether to continue, modify, or discontinue current regimen.

faqs.title: Structured monitoring protocol for all patients on stimulants
faqs.first_layer_html:
Cardiovascular monitoring cadence

WhenWhat to check
Baseline (before continuing or initiating)BP, pulse, weight
After dose changesBP and pulse at each adjustment
Stable patientsBP, pulse, weight every 6 months
CV risk factors / borderline readingsBP and pulse every 3 months

Action thresholds

  • Sustained resting HR >120 bpm → dose reduction + specialist referral
  • SBP ≥140/90 on two separate occasions → dose reduction + specialist referral
  • Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90) at baseline → defer dose escalation until controlled
  • Hypertensive crisis (≥180/120) → absolute contraindication
Note: ECG is not routinely required. Obtain only when personal or family history suggests cardiac disease.

sub_questions.question: What cardiac history requires pre-prescribing cardiology workup?
sub_questions.answer_html: Personal history: structural heart disease, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, CAD, prior MI, or Wolff-Parkinson-White. Family history: sudden cardiac death, ventricular arrhythmia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome. Symptom triggers: exertional chest pain, unexplained syncope, exertional dyspnea, palpitations.

sub_questions.question: What does the long-term cardiovascular risk evidence say?
sub_questions.answer_html: A large Swedish study (n≈278,000, 14-year follow-up) found a small but real incremental cardiovascular risk during the first ~3 years of stimulant exposure (~4% increased CVD risk per year), then a plateau.[ref:jama-psych-zhang2024] The signal was driven by hypertension and arterial disease — no increased risk of arrhythmia, heart failure, ischemic heart disease, or stroke. Risk became significant only at ≥1.5× defined daily dose (e.g., methylphenidate ≥45 mg/day). Counsel patients on modest, dose-dependent, blood-pressure-mediated cardiovascular risk.

sub_questions.question: Should I switch to a nonstimulant to reduce cardiovascular risk?
sub_questions.answer_html: Not on cardiovascular grounds alone. Atomoxetine and viloxazine produce blood-pressure and heart-rate effects of comparable magnitude to stimulants.[ref:lancet-psych-farhat2025] Guanfacine is the only ADHD agent associated with decreased BP and pulse (mean SBP −10 mmHg, DBP −8 mmHg, HR −7 bpm) and may be considered when cardiovascular concerns limit stimulant continuation — but this typically warrants specialist input.

faqs.title: Patient requesting combination or second stimulant
faqs.first_layer_html:
A long-acting + same-class short-acting booster (e.g., Adderall XR + dextroamphetamine IR, or Concerta + methylphenidate IR) is a routine end-of-dose strategy — not specialist-only territory. No US guideline restricts same-class booster prescribing to specialists.[ref:cortese-cns-2021]

Combination type vs. scope

CombinationScope
Same-class LA + IR booster (e.g., Concerta + MPH IR)Primary care scope — document cumulative dose and rationale
Cross-class (amphetamine + methylphenidate)Uncommon; warrants specialist input
Stimulant + alpha-agonist or atomoxetineCross-class polypharmacy; warrants specialist input

The honest guardrail is competency-based: "Am I comfortable with the combination dosing and monitoring?" — not "Am I allowed to prescribe this?"

sub_questions.question: The patient had a booster prescribed before and wants to restart it.
sub_questions.answer_html: Restarting a previously prescribed regimen is lower-risk than initiating something new, but treat that as clinical convention, not a guideline-graded distinction. Supportive factors: prior documentation, PDMP confirmation of previous dispensing and tolerability, non-clinical reason for discontinuation (provider change, insurance). Caveats: prior tolerability doesn't guarantee current safety; reassess BP, HR, and psychiatric status before restarting. If the prior record shows the combination was safe and discontinued for a non-clinical reason, continuation with fresh documentation is defensible.

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Patient requesting addition of [agent] to current stimulant regimen. Requesting specialist input on appropriateness and monitoring.

modules.landing_intro: A patient has a low hemoglobin. The reflex to immediately consult hematology is understandable — but a hematologist receiving a referral with only a CBC and no workup cannot do much from a distance. Your job is to complete a structured initial evaluation that answers the first-order question: what kind of anemia is this? Most anemia seen in primary care has a diagnosable and treatable cause that does not require hematology at all. For those that do, arriving with a completed workup transforms the consult from a hand-off into a collaboration.
modules.checklist_section_label: Before you escalate — complete all four

checklist.statement: CBC with differential reviewed — MCV categorized as microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic
Reticulocyte count obtained — production vs. destruction vs. loss established
Iron studies obtained if microcytic or mixed — serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation
B12 and folate obtained if macrocytic or normocytic with clinical suspicion

green_zone.zone_label: All boxes checked — You have a working diagnosis
green_zone.narrative_html: Initial workup complete. You can now categorize and begin treating the most common causes — iron deficiency, B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, or anemia of chronic disease — without hematology involvement. Document findings and plan using SmartPhrase below. Hematology consult is indicated only for unexplained, refractory, or complex findings. You are institutionally supported.

modules.escalation_section_label: Escalate to hematology consult if any apply

escalation.statement: Hemoglobin < 7 g/dL or symptomatic at any level (chest pain, dyspnea at rest, hemodynamic instability)
Workup complete — no etiology identified after iron studies, B12, folate, reticulocyte count, and clinical review
Evidence of hemolysis — elevated LDH, elevated indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count without blood loss
Abnormal WBC or platelet count accompanying anemia — pancytopenia, blasts on differential, or thrombocytopenia without explanation
Iron deficiency anemia not responding to 3 months of adequate oral iron replacement
Anemia in setting of CKD G3b or above — see Meridian CKD module for coordinated workup

modules.footer_note: For internal use only. This is a viable first pathway, not the only pathway. Experienced providers retain clinical discretion. Urgent findings — schistocytes, blasts, severe symptomatic anemia — require same-day escalation outside this consult framework.

faqs.title: Reading the CBC — MCV as your first branch point

items.question: What MCV thresholds define the categories?
items.answer_html:
Standard laboratory reference ranges:

Microcytic: MCV < 80 fL — think iron deficiency first, then thalassemia, then anemia of chronic disease (can be microcytic), then sideroblastic anemia (rare).

Normocytic: MCV 80–100 fL — think anemia of chronic disease, early iron deficiency, renal anemia, hypothyroidism, mixed deficiency, or early bone marrow pathology.

Macrocytic: MCV > 100 fL — think B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, hypothyroidism, alcohol use, medications (methotrexate, hydroxyurea, zidovudine), or myelodysplastic syndrome in older patients.

MCV is your first branch point. Every subsequent test order flows from this categorization.

items.question: The MCV is normal but the hemoglobin is low. Does that mean it's anemia of chronic disease?
items.answer_html:
Normocytic anemia is the broadest category and requires the most differential thinking. Anemia of chronic disease is common but should be a diagnosis of context — meaning the patient has a known chronic inflammatory condition (rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, malignancy, CKD) that explains it.

Normocytic anemia without a clear chronic disease context requires reticulocyte count as the next step to distinguish between underproduction and loss or destruction.

items.question: The RDW is elevated. What does that tell me?
items.answer_html:
Elevated RDW (red cell distribution width) indicates anisocytosis — a mixed population of cell sizes. This is particularly useful in two scenarios:

(1) A microcytic anemia with high RDW suggests iron deficiency rather than thalassemia (thalassemia tends to have normal or low RDW despite low MCV).

(2) A normocytic anemia with high RDW may indicate a mixed deficiency — iron plus B12 or folate — where the two processes cancel each other out in terms of MCV while the RDW reflects the heterogeneity. When the MCV looks normal but the RDW is high, order both iron studies and B12/folate.

items.question: Should I be looking at the differential on every anemia CBC?
items.answer_html:
Yes — the differential provides information the MCV alone cannot. Hypersegmented neutrophils (≥ 5 lobes) are a classic finding in B12 or folate deficiency and may precede macrocytosis. Target cells suggest hemoglobinopathy or liver disease.

Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) indicate microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — TTP, HUS, DIC — and are an emergency finding. If you see schistocytes on a differential, escalate immediately.

faqs.title: Production vs. destruction vs. loss — why this test matters

items.question: What does the reticulocyte count tell me that the CBC doesn't?
items.answer_html: The reticulocyte count tells you what the bone marrow is doing in response to the anemia. A normal bone marrow facing anemia should increase production — reticulocytes should rise. If they don't, the problem is in the bone marrow or in the substrate (iron, B12, folate). If they are elevated, the marrow is responding appropriately, which means the problem is peripheral — blood loss or destruction (hemolysis).

items.question: How do I interpret the reticulocyte count correctly?
items.answer_html:
Use the reticulocyte production index (RPI) rather than the raw reticulocyte percentage, which is misleading in anemia because it is expressed as a percentage of a smaller RBC pool:

RPI = (reticulocyte % × patient hematocrit) ÷ 45

RPI < 2: hypoproliferative — bone marrow is not responding appropriately. Think iron deficiency, B12/folate deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, renal anemia, or bone marrow pathology.

RPI > 2: hyperproliferative — marrow is responding. Think hemolysis or acute blood loss.

items.question: I ordered a reticulocyte count and it came back as a percentage only. Is that enough?
items.answer_html:
A raw percentage without the RPI calculation is limited — you need to interpret it in context. A reticulocyte percentage of 2.5% sounds elevated but may represent an RPI of 1.2 in a severely anemic patient, indicating an inadequate response.

Do the RPI calculation yourself using the formula above and document it in the note.

faqs.title: Iron deficiency — diagnosing and treating correctly

items.question: What is the most reliable test for iron deficiency?
items.answer_html:
Ferritin is the most sensitive single marker for iron deficiency when low — a ferritin < 30 ng/mL is highly specific for iron deficiency in most clinical contexts. However, ferritin is an acute phase reactant and is elevated by inflammation, infection, liver disease, and malignancy.

A patient with an inflammatory condition can have a ferritin of 80 ng/mL and still be iron deficient. In the context of chronic inflammation, a ferritin up to 100 ng/mL does not exclude iron deficiency — transferrin saturation < 20% in this context supports the diagnosis. Use the full panel: serum iron, TIBC, ferritin, and transferrin saturation together.

items.question: I've confirmed iron deficiency. How do I treat it?
items.answer_html:
Oral iron is first-line for most patients:

Ferrous sulfate 325 mg (65 mg elemental iron) every other day — as effective as daily dosing with significantly fewer GI side effects. This is a meaningful recent evidence update from the older twice-daily standard.

Take on an empty stomach with vitamin C (orange juice) to maximize absorption. Avoid within 2 hours of calcium, antacids, PPIs, or thyroid medication.

Recheck CBC and reticulocyte count in 4 weeks — you should see reticulocyte response within 1–2 weeks and hemoglobin rise of 1–2 g/dL by 4 weeks if the diagnosis and absorption are correct.

Continue treatment for 3 months after hemoglobin normalizes to replete stores.

items.question: My patient cannot tolerate oral iron or has a PPI she won't stop. What are my options?
items.answer_html:
IV iron is appropriate and effective for patients with malabsorption, intolerance to oral iron, inflammatory bowel disease, or who are on PPIs that cannot be discontinued. IV iron formulations (ferric carboxymaltose, low molecular weight iron dextran, ferumoxytol) can be administered in an infusion center.

This is within primary care scope to order — you do not need hematology referral to initiate IV iron in uncomplicated iron deficiency anemia.

items.question: I found iron deficiency. Do I need to find the source?
items.answer_html:
In most cases yes — iron deficiency in an adult is blood loss until proven otherwise. In premenopausal women with heavy menstrual bleeding, the source is often clinically apparent and colonoscopy is not mandatory in the absence of GI symptoms or red flags.

In men and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency requires GI evaluation — upper endoscopy and colonoscopy — to exclude occult GI blood loss including malignancy. Do not treat iron deficiency in a postmenopausal woman or any man without addressing the question of GI source.

items.question: Ferritin is 150 and transferrin saturation is 15%. Is this iron deficiency?
items.answer_html:
Possibly — this pattern (normal or elevated ferritin, low transferrin saturation) in the context of chronic inflammation is called functional iron deficiency or iron-restricted erythropoiesis. The iron exists in stores but is not being released for use. This is distinct from absolute iron deficiency and is the hallmark of anemia of chronic disease with iron restriction.

Treatment depends on the underlying condition — treating the inflammation is the primary intervention, supplemental iron has limited benefit in pure anemia of chronic disease, and IV iron may be considered in select cases (particularly CKD — see CKD module).

faqs.title: Macrocytic anemia — deficiencies and their distinctions

items.question: When should I order B12 and folate?
items.answer_html: Always order both when MCV > 100. Also consider ordering in: normocytic anemia with elevated RDW, hypersegmented neutrophils on differential, neurological symptoms (peripheral neuropathy, cognitive change, balance problems), history of gastric bypass or significant GI resection, strict vegan diet without supplementation, chronic PPI use (reduces B12 absorption over years), metformin use (reduces B12 absorption — check annually in long-term users), or active alcohol use disorder.

items.question: The B12 level is 250 pg/mL — normal range starts at 200. Is this enough to exclude deficiency?
items.answer_html:
No — serum B12 is an unreliable marker at the low-normal range. Levels between 200–400 pg/mL can be associated with functional deficiency, particularly in symptomatic patients.

If clinical suspicion is present, order methylmalonic acid (MMA) and homocysteine — both are elevated in B12 deficiency and are more sensitive markers of functional deficiency than serum B12 alone. A normal MMA effectively excludes B12 deficiency regardless of the serum level.

items.question: I've confirmed B12 deficiency. Do I need to find the cause before treating?
items.answer_html:
Treat first, investigate in parallel. B12 deficiency with neurological symptoms is a semi-urgent treatment situation — neurological damage from B12 deficiency can be permanent if prolonged. Initiate replacement immediately.

The most common cause in older adults is pernicious anemia (autoimmune gastritis with intrinsic factor deficiency) — check anti-intrinsic factor antibody and anti-parietal cell antibody. If pernicious anemia is confirmed, parenteral B12 (IM cyanocobalamin) is traditionally used, though high-dose oral B12 (1000–2000 mcg daily) is absorbed adequately via passive diffusion even without intrinsic factor and is now considered equivalent by most guidelines.

items.question: Folate is low. Is the workup the same as B12?
items.answer_html:
Folate deficiency is simpler in etiology — it is almost always dietary (poor intake, alcohol use disorder, malabsorption) or medication-related (methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin). Unlike B12 deficiency, folate deficiency does not cause neurological symptoms — if a macrocytic anemia patient has neurological symptoms, look harder at B12 regardless of folate level.

Treatment is oral folic acid 1 mg daily. Identify and address the underlying cause — folate deficiency in a patient not on a causative medication should prompt dietary and alcohol use assessment.

items.question: My patient is on methotrexate and has macrocytic anemia. Is this just expected?
items.answer_html:
Methotrexate causes macrocytosis by folate antagonism — this is an expected pharmacological effect and does not necessarily indicate deficiency or require dose change. However, if the anemia is significant or the patient is symptomatic, check folate level and ensure they are on folic acid supplementation (standard with methotrexate therapy).

Coordinate with the prescribing provider before making changes to the methotrexate regimen.

faqs.title: When anemia is urgent — thresholds and immediate management

items.question: What are the symptoms that make any hemoglobin level urgent?
items.answer_html:
Chest pain, dyspnea at rest, tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, or altered mental status in the context of anemia require same-day evaluation regardless of the absolute hemoglobin level.

A patient with hemoglobin of 9 g/dL who is having chest pain and tachycardia is more urgent than a patient with hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL who is ambulatory and asymptomatic. Symptoms drive urgency more than numbers.

items.question: At what hemoglobin level should I be considering transfusion?
items.answer_html:
Transfusion thresholds in stable outpatients:

Hemoglobin < 7 g/dL — transfusion is generally indicated in symptomatic patients. In asymptomatic, young, otherwise healthy patients with a clearly reversible cause (iron deficiency being actively treated), watchful waiting with close monitoring is sometimes appropriate — discuss with hematology.

Hemoglobin 7–8 g/dL — transfusion guided by symptoms and underlying condition. Patients with cardiac disease or limited cardiopulmonary reserve may need transfusion at higher thresholds.

Hemoglobin > 8 g/dL — transfusion rarely indicated in stable outpatients without active bleeding or severe symptoms.

Outpatient transfusion can be arranged through infusion centers — this does not require ER admission for a stable but significantly anemic patient.

items.question: The patient has hemoglobin of 6.8 and is mildly symptomatic on exertion. Do I send them to the ER?
items.answer_html:
Not necessarily — if the patient is stable, ambulatory, not having chest pain or tachycardia, and you can arrange outpatient transfusion within 24–48 hours, this is manageable without an ER visit. Call the infusion center, arrange the transfusion, and ensure the patient has clear return precautions.

If outpatient transfusion cannot be arranged promptly or the patient's condition is at all unstable, send to the ER with a direct communication to the receiving team.

faqs.title: Workup complete — still no answer

items.question: I've done the full initial workup and I can't explain the anemia. What have I potentially missed?
items.answer_html:
Review this list before the consult:

Hypothyroidism — TSH should be part of any unexplained normocytic or macrocytic anemia workup.

Renal insufficiency — check creatinine and eGFR; anemia of CKD is common and underrecognized.

Chronic liver disease — LFTs, consider hepatitis screening.

Lead toxicity — in patients with occupational exposure, recent immigration from high-exposure regions, or pica; order blood lead level.

Medication review — many drugs cause anemia through various mechanisms; review the full medication list.

Alcohol use — often underreported; ask directly.

Inflammatory markers — ESR, CRP, ferritin as acute phase reactant; anemia of chronic inflammation may not have an obvious clinical source.

items.question: What does the hematology consult ask look like for unexplained anemia?
items.answer_html:
Be specific and include your workup: "Patient with [degree] [MCV category] anemia, hemoglobin [X]. Workup completed: iron studies [results], B12 [result], folate [result], reticulocyte count/RPI [result], TSH [result], CMP [result]. No clear etiology identified. No evidence of hemolysis. CBC differential without abnormal forms. Requesting evaluation for underlying cause and management recommendation."

A hematologist receiving this consult can move directly to the next tier of evaluation rather than repeating your workup.

faqs.title: When the marrow is working but the cells are being destroyed

items.question: What lab pattern confirms hemolysis?
items.answer_html:
The hemolysis panel: elevated LDH (released from lysed RBCs), elevated indirect bilirubin (from heme catabolism), low or undetectable haptoglobin (binds free hemoglobin and is consumed), and elevated reticulocyte count/RPI (marrow responding to peripheral destruction).

Not all markers need to be abnormal simultaneously — low haptoglobin alone has high specificity for hemolysis. Order the full panel and document which markers are positive.

items.question: I have confirmed hemolysis. What are the common causes I should consider before hematology?
items.answer_html:
Categorize by mechanism:

Immune-mediated — warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). Order direct antiglobulin test (DAT/Coombs). A positive DAT confirms immune-mediated destruction and is the most common cause of hemolysis in primary care patients. Associated with autoimmune conditions, CLL, and certain medications (methyldopa, penicillin, cephalosporins).

Microangiopathic — schistocytes on smear: TTP, HUS, DIC, malignant hypertension. This is an emergency — do not manage outpatient.

Hereditary — G6PD deficiency (often triggered by infection, oxidative drugs, fava beans — order G6PD level), hereditary spherocytosis (spherocytes on smear, family history), sickle cell disease (usually known).

items.question: I see schistocytes on the peripheral smear. What do I do?
items.answer_html:
Treat as urgent. Schistocytes indicate microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — RBCs being sheared by damaged small vessels. TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) is life-threatening and time-sensitive — check platelet count immediately.

Thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is TTP until proven otherwise and requires same-day hematology contact, not an consult. Send the patient to the ER with a direct communication.

faqs.title: When anemia is part of a bigger picture

items.question: The CBC shows anemia plus thrombocytopenia. What does that mean?
items.answer_html:
Bicytopenia (two cell lines low) is a more concerning finding than isolated anemia. The differential includes: bone marrow failure (aplastic anemia), infiltrative bone marrow process (hematologic malignancy, metastatic solid tumor), hypersplenism, autoimmune destruction of multiple cell lines, B12/folate deficiency (can cause pancytopenia), or medications (chemotherapy, immunosuppressants, some antibiotics).

This requires hematology consult — not after a prolonged workup, but promptly.

items.question: The differential mentions "atypical lymphocytes." How concerned should I be?
items.answer_html:
Context matters. Atypical lymphocytes are common in viral infections — EBV (infectious mononucleosis), CMV, and other viral syndromes produce reactive atypical lymphocytes that are benign and self-limited. In a young patient with fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy, check monospot and EBV titers.

In an older patient without a viral prodrome, persistent atypical lymphocytes or a lymphocytosis that doesn't resolve warrants hematology consult to evaluate for lymphoproliferative disease.

items.question: The report says "blasts seen." What do I do?
items.answer_html:
Contact hematology today — do not wait for an consult response. Blasts on a peripheral smear suggest acute leukemia until proven otherwise. This is a same-day phone call to hematology, not a portal message.

While arranging urgent evaluation, do not start any new medications that could affect the marrow picture. Be direct with the patient that you have found something that requires urgent specialist evaluation.

faqs.title: Not responding to oral iron — what to do next

items.question: How do I know if the oral iron trial has been adequate?
items.answer_html:
An adequate trial requires: correct diagnosis (confirmed iron deficiency, not anemia of chronic disease), correct dose (ferrous sulfate 325 mg on alternate days or equivalent), correct administration (empty stomach, with vitamin C, away from PPIs and calcium), and sufficient duration (minimum 4 weeks for reticulocyte response, 8–12 weeks for meaningful hemoglobin rise).

Before calling a trial a failure, verify all four. The most common reason for apparent treatment failure is PPI use that was not addressed.

items.question: I've confirmed adequate trial and there's been no response. What are the possibilities?
items.answer_html:
Ongoing blood loss exceeding replacement — the source has not been identified or is continuing. Malabsorption — celiac disease, gastric bypass, inflammatory bowel disease, H. pylori gastritis. Incorrect diagnosis — reconsider whether this is truly iron deficiency or functional iron deficiency in the context of inflammation.

H. pylori infection specifically is associated with refractory iron deficiency anemia and should be tested if not already done (urea breath test or stool antigen).

items.question: When is IV iron the right answer for refractory cases?
items.answer_html:
IV iron is appropriate when oral iron has genuinely failed after an adequate trial, when malabsorption is confirmed or strongly suspected, when the patient cannot tolerate oral iron, or when rapid repletion is needed (preoperative optimization, severe symptomatic anemia).

IV iron does not require hematology referral — it can be ordered by primary care and administered in an infusion center. Refractory iron deficiency that fails IV iron, or iron deficiency without an identified source in a patient who has had appropriate GI evaluation, is the threshold for hematology consult.

faqs.title: Renal anemia — coordination with the CKD module

items.question: How is anemia of CKD different from other anemias?
items.answer_html:
Anemia of CKD is normocytic and normochromic, caused primarily by reduced erythropoietin production by the damaged kidneys. It typically becomes clinically apparent at eGFR < 45 (G3b) and is nearly universal at G4–G5.

It is a diagnosis of exclusion in the context of CKD — meaning iron deficiency, B12 deficiency, and other causes should be ruled out before attributing anemia solely to CKD. Many CKD patients have coexisting iron deficiency that is treatable and should be corrected before considering erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.

items.question: My CKD patient has anemia. What workup do I do?
items.answer_html:
Complete the standard Meridian anemia workup first — CBC with differential, reticulocyte count, iron studies, B12, folate. Additionally order PTH, phosphorus, and 25-OH vitamin D if not recently done as part of CKD mineral metabolism assessment.

Then cross-reference with the Meridian CKD module for integrated management. The CKD consult to nephrology should include the anemia workup so the nephrologist can advise on ESA candidacy with complete information.

items.question: Should I start an ESA (erythropoiesis-stimulating agent)?
items.answer_html:
ESA initiation is a nephrology decision in the primary care context. Your role is to identify the anemia, complete the workup, correct any iron deficiency (IV iron preferred in CKD — oral iron is poorly absorbed in CKD patients and worsens constipation), and document.

Do not initiate ESA therapy without nephrology input — ESAs carry risks including accelerated cardiovascular events and increased tumor progression risk in malignancy, and dosing requires monitoring that is typically managed by nephrology.

modules.default_title: Abdominal Pain — Can I discharge this patient?
modules.landing_intro: A patient presents to urgent care with abdominal pain. Our job — in 15–20 minutes — is to decide between safe discharge, close-interval re-evaluation, or ER transfer. This checklist supports that decision after a focused H&P and any reasonable rapid testing. ER referral with a reasonable workup is always appropriate and is never penalized. The only penalty is no workup at all.
modules.checklist_section_label: Before you discharge — verify all four

checklist.statement: Vitals and clinical appearance are reassuring — no fever > 101.3°F, not persistently tachycardic, tolerates oral intake, ambulates, and pain is controlled on oral analgesia
No peritoneal signs on exam — no rebound, involuntary guarding, rigidity, marked distention, or pulsatile mass
Labs, if drawn, are reassuring — no severe leukocytosis or left shift, CRP < 50 mg/L, lipase < 3× upper limit of normal — or labs were not clinically indicated
Imaging, if performed, shows no findings requiring urgent intervention — or imaging was not clinically indicated for this presentation

green_zone.zone_label: All four boxes checked — Discharge with ER precautions and 24-hour re-evaluation
green_zone.narrative_html:
Disposition supported: discharge home with ER-precautions return instructions and a scheduled re-evaluation within 24–30 hours (in-house PCP visit, structured telephone callback, or a planned UC return). The follow-up is not optional — it's the safety net that makes same-visit discharge defensible. Roughly 20–25% of non-specific abdominal pain patients have a diagnostic change at re-evaluation (Boendermaker 2018), and that structured return is what catches the ones the first visit missed.

Explicit return precautions — written and read back: worsening or migrating pain, vomiting blood, bloody or black stools, new fever, inability to tolerate fluids, fainting, or any change in mental status. Any of these → ER, not back to UC.

Documentation: use the SmartPhrase below — it captures the four-point rubric, the negatives, the return precautions, and the follow-up arrangement. ER referral with a reasonable workup is always appropriate. The only penalty is no workup.

modules.escalation_section_label: Transfer to ER or call surgeon immediately if any apply

escalation.statement: Hemodynamic instability — hypotension, persistent tachycardia despite fluids, altered mental status, or signs of sepsis
Peritoneal signs or rigid abdomen — suspected perforation, peritonitis, or ischemic bowel
Pain out of proportion to exam — especially in elderly, atrial fibrillation, or post-prandial patterns (mesenteric ischemia)
Sudden-onset excruciating pain — perforation, AAA rupture, aortic dissection, ovarian or testicular torsion

context_strip.label: Urgent care throughput
context_strip.text: Target visit 15–20 minutes. Current average ~30. ER referral with a reasonable workup is never penalized — over-workup is the hidden cost.

modules.footer_note: First-draft v1 — dedicated sub-modules for pregnancy / women of childbearing age, pediatric, and geriatric abdominal pain are planned. Iteration welcomed.

faqs.title: What 'reassuring' actually means — and why pediatrics is different

items.question: What counts as reassuring vitals and appearance?
items.answer_html:
Temperature: no fever > 101.3°F (38.5°C). A low-grade temp in a well-appearing adult is not a discharge-blocker on its own, but document and factor it in.

Heart rate: not persistently tachycardic after analgesia and fluids. Pain and anxiety drive HR; a tachycardia that does not respond to a reasonable intervention is a yellow flag.

Blood pressure: at baseline. Normotension with the patient's known baseline counts.

Appearance: tolerating oral intake, ambulating, pain controlled on oral analgesia. The patient who can't sit up for a pretzel and a sip of water is not going home on oral ibuprofen.

The underlying principle is trajectory: the patient you're about to discharge should look better than they did walking in, not the same.

items.question: A single borderline vital — does it flip the decision?
items.answer_html:
Not on its own. One isolated vital needs a reason and a recheck:

HR 105 on arrival — recheck after analgesia + 500 mL NS. If it normalizes, that's a pain/volume signal, not a disease signal.

Temp 100.9°F — combine with the rest of the picture. Febrile + RLQ pain + elevated WBC is a different patient than febrile + URI + diffuse abdominal discomfort.

Persistent tachycardia despite intervention — move toward the red zone. This is the signal that shouldn't be ignored.

Document the recheck. A single captured vital without a second look is a malpractice exposure, not a clinical decision.

items.question: What about children? (stub — dedicated pediatric module planned)
items.answer_html:
The adult rubric does not apply directly to children. A pediatric abdominal pain module is on the roadmap. Key differences to keep in mind in the meantime:

• Pediatric vitals are age-dependent — a HR of 140 is different at 2 years old than at 20. Use age-normed tables, not adult ranges.

• Classic pediatric red flags: bilious emesis (any age → surgical until proven otherwise), the intussusception triad (intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, currant-jelly stools — though most cases don't show the full triad), testicular exam in any boy with abdominal pain (torsion presents as abdominal pain), Henoch-Schönlein purpura with palpable purpura + abdominal pain.

• Dehydration assessment weighs heavier than in adults — capillary refill, mucous membranes, urine output, activity level.

• Lower threshold for PCP/ED handoff. If the in-house pediatrician is available, that's your partner; if not, a warm handoff to ED is the safer path in v1.

faqs.title: Reading the abdomen — guarding, rigidity, and what the cough test tells you

items.question: How do I differentiate voluntary from involuntary guarding?
items.answer_html:
Voluntary guarding softens with distraction. Talk to the patient, ask about their kids, bend their knees, re-approach the exam. If the abdominal wall relaxes when they're not thinking about it, it's voluntary — that's pain avoidance, not peritonitis.

Involuntary guarding does not relax. The abdominal wall stays tight regardless of distraction or positioning. That's a reflex arc from an irritated peritoneum — it's a sign, not a behavior.

Rigidity is the extreme end: a board-like abdomen that doesn't move with respiration. That patient is not going home — they're going to the ER or to your in-house surgeon.

items.question: What's the cough test, and why does it matter for urgent care?
items.answer_html:
Ask the patient to cough, or to jump/hop if they can tolerate it. Reproduction of focal abdominal pain with cough or jar is a reliable indicator of peritoneal irritation — it's the cheapest, fastest peritoneal-signs screen available and does not require you to touch the abdomen.

In a time-pressured UC environment, it's an efficient triage tool. A patient who jumps off the exam table cleanly is not peritonitic. A patient who winces and grabs their side with cough deserves a closer look.

items.question: Elderly and immunocompromised patients don't always mount a classic exam — what then?
items.answer_html:
Lower your threshold. Elderly, diabetic, and immunocompromised patients can have surgical abdomens without fever, without marked tenderness, and without classic guarding. The literature is consistent: atypical presentations are the norm, not the exception.

If the patient is age > 65, immunocompromised, on chronic steroids, or significantly obese, a normal-looking exam is less reassuring than it would be in a 30-year-old. Weight imaging more heavily, lower the bar for ER transfer, and do not let an unimpressive exam override the rest of the clinical picture.

See the elderly/immunocompromised stub under 'Pain out of proportion to exam' for more detail.

faqs.title: What to order, what the thresholds mean, and the pregnancy question

items.question: When are labs actually required vs. optional?
items.answer_html:
Labs are a tool, not a ritual. A well-appearing patient with a benign exam and a clear benign etiology (gastroenteritis that's improving, musculoskeletal wall tenderness, constipation with relief after bowel movement) does not automatically need a CBC + BMP + lipase + CRP. Order labs when they will change disposition, not to paper-chart a workup.

Order labs when:

• The diagnosis is uncertain and you're entertaining a surgical or infectious cause.

• The patient is in a higher-risk group (elderly, immunocompromised, diabetic) where the exam may underestimate severity.

• You need a negative result to support a discharge decision that would otherwise feel borderline.

Consider skipping labs when:

• The history and exam point convincingly to a benign etiology.

• The patient is well-appearing and the clinical trajectory is improving during observation.

A documented reasonable workup does not require every box checked — it requires the right boxes for this patient.

items.question: Where do the CRP < 50 and lipase < 3× ULN thresholds come from?
items.answer_html:
CRP < 50 mg/L: derived from emergency-medicine literature on non-specific abdominal pain discharge safety — values above 50 correlate with surgical pathology at meaningfully higher rates. This is an institution-calibrated number and should be treated as a decision aid, not a rule. A CRP of 55 in a well-appearing patient with an otherwise benign workup is different from a CRP of 55 with peritoneal signs.

Lipase < 3× ULN: the standard cutoff for excluding acute pancreatitis. Elevations in the 1–3× range can reflect non-specific inflammation, renal dysfunction, or other causes; > 3× is the action threshold. Pair with clinical picture — a painful patient with lipase 2.5× ULN still deserves a conversation with imaging or surgery.

Caveat: these thresholds are derived from adult, non-pregnant, general UC/ED populations. Special populations need different calibration.

items.question: Pregnancy / women of childbearing age — urine β-hCG vs. serum (stub — dedicated module planned)
items.answer_html:
Urine β-hCG is the workhorse in UC. Results in minutes, adequate sensitivity for the discharge-decision timeframe. A negative urine β-hCG in a woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain is generally sufficient to proceed down the general-adult discharge rubric, provided the rest of the picture is reassuring.

Serum quantitative β-hCG is orderable in-house, but turnaround is measured in hours. If ordered later in the day it may not result until the next day — it is not a real-time UC decision aid. Use serum when:

• Urine is positive and you need viability / ectopic workup (pair with pelvic US).

• Urine is negative but clinical suspicion for very early pregnancy is high enough that the sensitivity gap matters (i.e., you need a number, not a yes/no).

Document: what you ordered, the result, and whether the turnaround was compatible with a same-visit disposition. If you ordered serum late in the day knowing it wouldn't return, that needs a management plan (recheck tomorrow, ED referral, or scheduled return).

Ectopic must be actively considered in any positive-pregnancy woman with lower abdominal pain — in-house OB/GYN consult or ER transfer before discharge. A pregnant patient with abdominal pain is not a general-adult discharge case.

faqs.title: When to image, when not to, and how to document the choice

items.question: When is imaging actually indicated?
items.answer_html:
Imaging is indicated when the result will change disposition. Common UC scenarios where it will:

• RLQ pain with any concern for appendicitis — US first in children and thin adults; CT if US non-diagnostic or patient is obese.

• Flank pain with hematuria — non-contrast CT for stone evaluation.

• RUQ pain with Murphy's sign — US for cholecystitis.

• Suspected AAA — bedside US if available, CT with contrast otherwise.

• Post-operative or known-anatomy patients (hernias, prior bowel surgery) with pain — imaging nearly always indicated.

• Any patient where your gestalt is unsure and the patient is in a higher-risk group — elderly, immunocompromised, diabetic.

items.question: How do I document the rationale for NOT imaging?
items.answer_html:
The documentation for not imaging is as important as the documentation for imaging. Record:

• The differential you considered.

• The exam and lab findings that made a surgical or life-threatening cause unlikely.

• The specific return precautions given.

• The follow-up arrangement (who, when, how).

Example phrasing: "Considered appendicitis, cholecystitis, and diverticulitis; given benign exam without peritoneal signs, reassuring labs, and improvement with observation, imaging deferred. Patient instructed to return immediately for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, or inability to tolerate fluids; scheduled 24-hour phone re-evaluation."

A documented thought process is a defense. A sparse note is not.

items.question: What about the throughput cost of CT?
items.answer_html:
A same-visit CT with contrast in UC typically adds 45–90 minutes to the visit (IV placement, labs for creatinine if not already drawn, the scan itself, the read, and the clinician review). That's the difference between a 20-minute visit and a 90-minute visit.

CT is the right call when it will change disposition. It is the wrong call when it's being ordered to generate a negative result that wasn't going to change your plan anyway. 'Defensive imaging' is expensive — in time, in radiation, in patient throughput — and the cumulative cost at the clinic level is real.

If the question is 'do I need imaging to safely discharge,' the right answer is often a thoughtful re-exam and a scheduled re-evaluation rather than a scan.

faqs.title: Hemodynamic instability — logistics and stabilization

items.question: What are the logistics of ER transfer from UC?
items.answer_html:
Call EMS early. Don't wait for the patient to decompensate further. Once you've identified instability, the clock starts and the next task is transfer, not workup.

While EMS is en route: maintain IV access (two large-bore if possible), start fluid resuscitation, place on monitors (pulse ox, BP cycling, rhythm if available), obtain a focused last-round of vitals and a point-of-care glucose, and start the transfer documentation.

Call the receiving ER with a concise handoff: demographics, presentation, vitals trend, what you've done, what they're walking into. A 90-second phone call saves 30 minutes on the other end.

items.question: What can I actually do in UC before EMS arrives?
items.answer_html:
Available in most UCs: IV fluids (NS or LR boluses), supplemental O₂, broad-spectrum antibiotics if sepsis is the concern (don't wait for the ED to draw cultures — one dose started now is better than three hours later), analgesia appropriate to the picture, anti-emetics.

Not available: blood products, vasopressors, ICU-level monitoring, operative intervention, prolonged observation. If the patient needs any of those, the transfer is already the correct call.

faqs.title: Peritoneal signs — ER vs. in-house surgical path

items.question: Do I call our in-house general surgeon or send straight to the ER?
items.answer_html:
If the patient is unstable: ER. The in-house surgeon does not have ICU, anesthesia, or OR resources in our UC footprint.

If the patient is stable with clear surgical pathology (e.g., appendicitis on imaging, well-appearing, tolerating oral intake): a direct-to-surgeon conversation is reasonable and often faster. The surgeon can decide between same-day outpatient OR, ER admission via their service, or scheduled next-day surgery.

Err toward the ER when the picture is unclear or the patient's trajectory is uncertain. A surgical consult pathway is not a substitute for ED-level resources.

items.question: What can our in-house surgical capability actually do?
items.answer_html:
Available in-house: outpatient endoscopy, outpatient OR for elective or same-day straightforward cases, specialty consults (GI, urology, gynecology, general surgery) for same-day phone or in-person evaluation.

Not available in-house: cath lab, IR, ICU, regular hospital beds for observation or routine medical admission, blood banking, anesthesia support for emergent cases.

Translation: anything that needs admission, blood products, interventional radiology, or ICU-level monitoring goes to the ER regardless of how tightly coupled the surgical consult is.

faqs.title: Pain out of proportion — the one we miss

items.question: Why is mesenteric ischemia the classic 'miss' in abdominal pain?
items.answer_html:
Because the exam doesn't match the pain. Patients report severe, often excruciating pain — but the abdomen on exam is soft, minimally tender, no peritoneal signs. The reflex is to reassure: 'the exam is benign.' The reflex is wrong.

The classic triad — pain out of proportion to exam + a risk factor (AFib, recent MI, heart failure, hypercoagulable state, vasculopathy, age > 65) + metabolic acidosis on labs (if drawn) — is a transfer. Lactate, if available, is helpful but absence of elevation does not rule it out.

Post-prandial pattern — worse after eating, often with weight loss from food avoidance — suggests chronic mesenteric ischemia. Still a transfer for workup, just a different urgency profile.

If your gestalt is that the patient is more uncomfortable than the exam suggests, and they have a vascular risk profile: transfer. Don't let a soft belly reassure you.

items.question: Elderly, immunocompromised, obese — lower threshold across the board (stub — dedicated geriatric module planned)
items.answer_html:
These three groups all fail the classic rubric: atypical presentations, muted exams, normal-range vitals masking real pathology.

• Age > 65: vascular causes (mesenteric ischemia, AAA), perforated viscus without classic peritoneal signs, diverticulitis with atypical location. Mortality for a missed surgical abdomen in elderly patients is substantially higher than in younger patients — the discharge threshold should reflect that.

• Immunocompromised (chronic steroids, active chemo, transplant, advanced HIV, uncontrolled diabetes): can have surgical abdomens without fever, without leukocytosis, without marked tenderness. Treat exam and labs as less sensitive than in the general adult population.

• Obese patients: exam is genuinely harder, imaging is more often necessary, and BMI > 35 is independently associated with delayed diagnosis in abdominal pain literature.

Practical rule in v1: in any of these groups, imaging has a lower threshold, a negative workup is less reassuring, and 'discharge with 24-hour follow-up' needs a tighter follow-up loop (phone call, not hope). A dedicated geriatric/immunocompromised module is on the roadmap.

faqs.title: Thunderclap abdominal pain — the differential

items.question: What's the differential for sudden-onset, excruciating abdominal pain?
items.answer_html:
Pain that starts at maximum intensity — the patient can name the minute it began — is a different animal from pain that built up over hours.

Vascular catastrophes: AAA rupture (older patient, male, hypotension, pulsatile mass or back pain), aortic dissection (tearing pain, often radiating to the back, pulse differential between arms).

Perforated viscus: perforated ulcer, perforated diverticulum, perforated appendicitis. Pain often generalizes rapidly from a focal onset; free air on imaging.

Torsion: ovarian torsion (reproductive-age female, sudden pelvic pain ± nausea/vomiting), testicular torsion (any male with abdominal pain — check the testicles), volvulus in elderly patients.

Acute mesenteric ischemia: can present as sudden onset in embolic disease (AFib patient with sudden severe pain).

Ruptured ectopic: reproductive-age female with positive β-hCG, sudden pain, hemodynamic changes. See the pregnancy stub under Labs.

All of these are ER transfers — not UC workups.

items.question: How is this different from gradual-onset severe pain?
items.answer_html:
Gradual-onset severe pain still has a differential that includes surgical emergencies (appendicitis, cholecystitis, bowel obstruction), but the tempo allows more of a UC workup — imaging, labs, observation — before committing to disposition.

Sudden-onset does not. The tempo itself is diagnostic, and the workup needs to happen in an environment with full resources. Transfer, then workup.

Document the timeline carefully: time of onset, what the patient was doing, whether pain was at maximum intensity immediately. That single data point — 'pain started suddenly at maximum intensity at 2:15 PM' — is often what drives the escalation decision.

decision_tree.question: Is the patient on chronic opioid therapy (≥ 90 days) or at ≥ 50 MME/day?
decision_tree.hint: CDC 2022 flags chronic high-MME regimens for review and consideration of specialist input. Below this threshold, pain-medicine consult is rarely the right next step.
decision_tree.block_text: Pain medicine consult is generally reserved for chronic and/or higher-dose regimens. For acute pain or short-course prescribing, the answer is usually within PCP scope.

decision_tree.question: Is the patient stable on the current regimen with adequate function and no concerning PDMP/UDS findings?
decision_tree.hint: Stable, functional patients with inherited high-MME regimens are appropriate for PCP continuation with documented rationale — pain-medicine input is for sequencing or de-escalation guidance, not authorization to continue.

decision_tree.question: Are there active concerns — uncontrolled pain, functional decline, PDMP/UDS red flags, or concurrent benzodiazepines?
decision_tree.block_text: If the regimen is stable AND there are no concerns, continue PCP management. Pain medicine is not a routine annual touch-point in current guidelines.

consults.label: Addiction medicine consult
consults.blurb: Suspected OUD, MOUD/OAT initiation, aberrant behavior workup.

decision_tree.question: Are there signs concerning for opioid use disorder (DSM-5 criteria, aberrant behavior, escalation despite no nociceptive driver, or PDMP pattern suggesting misuse)?
decision_tree.hint: OUD signs do not bar continued prescribing — they signal the need for specialist co-management, not abrupt discontinuation.
decision_tree.block_text: Without OUD concerns, addiction medicine isn't the right consult. If chronic high-MME with stability concerns, pain medicine is the better path.

decision_tree.question: Is the patient already on MOUD (buprenorphine, methadone, naltrexone)?
decision_tree.hint: If yes, the consult question is around co-management of pain and OUD; if no, it's about initiation.

modules.landing_intro: A patient is transferring to your panel on a chronic opiate regimen. Your job at the first visit is not to solve the problem — it is to establish the relationship, complete a structured assessment, and determine whether you can continue, need to modify, or need to escalate. Do not discontinue at the first visit without a safety plan in place. CDC 2022 is explicit: opioid therapy should not be discontinued abruptly, and abrupt taper of long-stable patients is associated with overdose, mental-health crisis, and suicide attempt.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:agnoli-jama-2021] Tap any item for guidance.
modules.checklist_section_label: Before you decide — verify all four

checklist.statement: PDMP reviewed — single prescriber, single pharmacy, consistent quantities, no concurrent controlled substances of concern
Controlled substance agreement on file or completed at this visit — patient understands monitoring expectations
Urine drug screen obtained at intake — results reviewed and documented
Current MME calculated — dose documented, clinical rationale present for doses ≥50 MME/day

green_zone.narrative_html: Reasonable basis to continue the current regimen at this visit. PDMP reviewed, CS agreement in place, baseline UDS obtained, and MME documented with rationale. Schedule follow-up within 1–3 months — monitoring is ongoing, not a one-time clearance. Document using the SmartPhrase below. You are institutionally supported.

escalation.statement: Dose well above 50 MME/day without documented clinical rationale or functional benefit
Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription identified
UDS positive for a non-prescribed substance, or unexpectedly negative for the prescribed opiate
PDMP shows multiple prescribers, multiple pharmacies, or overlapping fills
Repeated early refill requests, lost medications, or escalating between-visit contact
Clinical concern for opioid use disorder

context_strip.label: About this framework
context_strip.text: This module supports the primary care provider at the inherited-patient first visit. It synthesizes the CDC 2022 opioid prescribing guideline, the ASAM/ACMT 2025 benzodiazepine tapering guideline, the VA/DoD 2022 chronic-pain guideline, and AAFP commentary; no single national source packages this scenario as a unified protocol.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:vadod-2022][ref:aafp-roth-2020] Numeric thresholds referenced here — early-refill ladders, UDS cadence tiers, the “three pharmacies” heuristic — reflect institutional convention informed by AAPM/APS expert consensus rather than specific CDC recommendations; CDC 2022 deliberately avoids rigid numeric thresholds.[ref:aapm-argoff-2018] PDMP requirements cited reflect New York (per-prescription under I-STOP) and New Jersey (initial plus quarterly under NJSA 45:1-46.1); providers in other states should verify their requirements with their compliance office.[ref:ny-pbh-3343a][ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1]

modules.footer_note: This module is advisory, not compulsory; experienced providers retain clinical discretion. Verify current state requirements with your compliance office, since controlled-substance regulations are subject to legislative updates.

faqs.title: What am I looking for in the PDMP for opiate patients?
faqs.first_layer_html:
How often must I check the PDMP?

StateRequired frequency
New York (I-STOP)Before every prescribing event — no exceptions[ref:ny-pbh-3343a]
New JerseyAt first prescription, then quarterly during ongoing therapy[ref:nj-njsa-45-1-46-1]
Other statesVerify with your compliance office

Top concerns, in priority order

  • Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription — associated with 2–5× overdose risk; requires documented risk–benefit assessment and naloxone (see Concurrent opiates and benzodiazepines).[ref:sun-bmj-2017][ref:hernandez-jamaopen-2018]
  • Overlapping fills from any prescriber — warrants clarification, not presumption of diversion; CDC 2022 explicitly notes that coordinated care may involve multiple prescribers.[ref:cdc-2022]
  • Multiple pharmacies — ≥4 pharmacies in 90 days is a research threshold; three is a reasonable clinical heuristic, not a validated cutoff.[ref:perry-add-2022]
  • Fill frequency vs. days-supply — a consistent pattern of early fills (e.g., a 30-day supply filled every 20 days) is more meaningful than an isolated instance; legitimate explanations include vacation, dose adjustments, and 14-day refills written as 30-day supply.
  • Cash-pay fills at multiple locations without explanation — pharmacies report all dispensed controlled substances to PDMPs regardless of payment method, so cash-pay alone is not the signal, but cash-pay without insurance at multiple locations warrants asking about.

Reassuring pattern: single prescriber, single pharmacy, consistent quantities, no concurrent controlled-substance prescriptions from other providers.

PDMP-generated algorithmic risk scores have not been validated against clinical outcomes and should not replace clinical judgment. CDC 2022 warns they can lead to stigmatization and may disparately affect women, persons of color, and persons living in poverty. A 10-year longitudinal analysis found traditional binary thresholds performed no better than chance at predicting OUD or overdose after 2015.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:perry-add-2022]

sub_questions.question: I see a second prescriber. Is that automatically a problem?
sub_questions.answer_html: No — the framing should be “warrants clarification,” not “suggests diversion.” CDC 2022 explicitly states that prescriptions may appropriately be written by more than one clinician coordinating care.[ref:cdc-2022] A PCP and a pain-management specialist co-managing a patient may have legitimate dual prescribing. Ask the patient directly, document the answer, and contact the other prescriber if the picture is unclear. Avoid the term “double-doctoring” in documentation until the pattern is confirmed as uncoordinated.

sub_questions.question: What do I document when I find a PDMP concern?
sub_questions.answer_html: Document exactly what you found (dates, prescribers, pharmacies, quantities), what you asked the patient, what they said, and your clinical assessment. If you continue prescribing despite a flag: document your reasoning, the patient’s explanation, steps taken to coordinate with other prescribers, and any monitoring intensifications. If you choose not to prescribe: document alternatives offered and the safety plan. Refusing to prescribe is defensible; refusing to provide any care pathway is not.[ref:cdc-2022]

faqs.title: The CS agreement — what it is and what it isn't
faqs.first_layer_html:
A new controlled substance agreement on prescriber-of-record transfer is strongly recommended best practice and, in many states, legally required. The prior agreement was between the patient and a different clinician — it does not bind the incoming prescriber. Completing a new agreement at the first visit is both a legal protection and a clinical moment: it lets you assess patient understanding and signals a managed therapeutic relationship.

A 2024 legal landscape review found 27 states mandate opioid treatment agreements with substantial variation in required terms; 23 states plus DC do not mandate by statute. Neither New York nor New Jersey independently mandates a written agreement by statute — in both states the requirement typically derives from institutional policy. Verify your institution’s specific standard.[ref:svirsky-milbank-2024]

Common elements (consensus-derived, not federally mandated)

  • Single prescriber, single pharmacy
  • UDS monitoring as clinically indicated
  • No early refills; no patient self-adjustment of dose
  • No replacement for lost or stolen medications (institutional policy, not federal regulation)
  • Functional improvement as the primary treatment goal — CDC 2022: “emphasize improvement in function as a primary goal; function can improve even when pain is not eliminated.” Clinically meaningful improvement is defined as ≥30% improvement in both pain and function (PEG scale).[ref:cdc-2022]
  • Safe storage and disposal obligations

CDC 2022 explicitly states it “did not find studies evaluating the effectiveness of written agreements or treatment plans.” These are consensus-derived risk-management provisions, not evidence-based mandates — label them accordingly in your own thinking.[ref:cdc-2022]

sub_questions.question: The patient refuses to sign. What do I do?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Ask why before responding — literacy barriers, language, prior negative experiences, and simply needing time to read are all common reasons. You are not obligated to prescribe without a signed agreement, and the institutional framework supports that position. However, CDC 2022 explicitly warns against patient abandonment: “Clinicians should avoid dismissing patients from care and should ensure appropriate care for patients with pain.”[ref:cdc-2022]

Document a four-element pattern: (1) the agreement was offered and explained with appropriate accommodations; (2) the patient declined, with their stated reason; (3) alternatives were offered — non-opioid pain management, pain-specialist referral, bridge prescription with short-interval follow-up; (4) the rationale for not prescribing the chronic opioid without the agreement.

faqs.title: UDS at intake — interpreting and acting on results
faqs.first_layer_html:
The point-of-care immunoassay (cup test) is a screen, not a verdict. CDC 2022 warns that “false positive and false negative presumptive results are not uncommon” and that clinicians commonly misinterpret results. All immunoassay results are presumptive until confirmed with GC-MS or LC-MS/MS.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:stolbach-jmt-2022]

Before you send the test: ask the patient, “If we test you today, what will we find? Will there be any surprises?” A candid answer can change how you interpret results and sometimes makes confirmatory testing unnecessary at that visit.

Interpreting a negative for the prescribed opiate — full differential

  • Wrong assay ordered — the most operationally important consideration. Standard “opiate” immunoassay panels do not detect oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, or buprenorphine. A patient on chronic oxycodone can return “no opiates detected” on a routine cup test, and that result is entirely expected given the assay. Verify the panel detects the prescribed agent before drawing conclusions.[ref:stolbach-jmt-2022][ref:mahajan-aa-2017]
  • Running out early due to undertreated pain — patient used more than prescribed; suggests the dose may be inadequate
  • Drug absent — used >72 hours ago; possible diversion, hoarding, or rapid metabolism
  • Specimen below assay cutoff — dose-timing artifact or PRN-use pattern
  • Specimen manipulation — dilution, adulteration, or synthetic urine substitution
  • Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus causing urine dilution
  • Pharmacogenetic anomaly or drug–drug interaction affecting metabolism
  • Laboratory error

Confirm with send-out testing where the result will change management. Have a direct, non-accusatory conversation: “I want to make sure we understand this result together before drawing any conclusions.”[ref:kale-aafp-2019]

sub_questions.question: How often should UDS be repeated after intake?
sub_questions.answer_html:
CDC 2022 recommends UDS “periodically (at least annually)” — it deliberately declined to specify risk-stratified cadence, noting that “predicting risk is challenging, and available tools do not allow clinicians to reliably identify patients at low risk.” The tiers below are institutional convention informed by AAPM/APS expert consensus.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aapm-argoff-2018]

Risk tierCadence
Stable (clean PDMP, signed agreement, no behavioral concerns)Every 6–12 months
Yellow flags presentEvery 3 months
Active concerns or recent escalationEvery visit until stable

Document your reasoning for the chosen interval. CMS and payer policies require documentation of medical necessity for definitive (send-out) testing.

For patients on multiple non-buprenorphine opiates, sum the per-agent MMEs. CDC notes “there is no single standard formula for calculating MMEs” — institutional variation exists and these are estimates.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:cdc-2016][ref:wen-jpm-2022]

Thresholds to know

  • ≥50 MME/day — the primary reassessment guidepost. Carefully reassess benefit vs. risk; increase follow-up frequency; offer naloxone. This is a clinical checkpoint, not a pharmacologic inflection point.[ref:cdc-2022]
  • Above 50 MME/day — risk increases continuously. Document clinical rationale for any dose above this guidepost. There is no CDC-specified numeric upper ceiling.
  • State-specific thresholds — some states impose their own numeric mandates (e.g., Washington requires pain-specialist consultation before exceeding 120 MME/day). Check your state’s requirements with your compliance office.

CDC 2022 frames overdose risk as continuous with dose, with no single safe threshold, and deliberately avoided specific numeric ceilings to prevent their use as “inflexible, rigid standards of care.”[ref:cdc-2022]

Naloxone — offer to any patient who meets any of these

  • ≥50 MME/day
  • Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription
  • History of substance use disorder or prior overdose
  • Sleep-disordered breathing
  • Post-incarceration release, or during/after tapering (lost tolerance to a prior dose)
  • Household members at risk of accidental exposure

Document that you offered or prescribed naloxone, counseled on administration, and confirmed household access.

sub_questions.question: The patient is on 120 MME/day and has been stable for years. Do I taper them?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Do not taper at the first visit. Stability on a long-standing dose is meaningful clinical data — but it is not a license for indefinite passive prescribing.

The harms of abrupt taper are well-quantified: Agnoli (JAMA 2021, n=113,618) found dose tapering of stable long-term patients associated with IRR 1.68 for overdose, 2.28 for mental-health crisis, and 3.30 for suicide attempt; absolute risk increases were largest at the highest baseline doses. CDC 2022 and the FDA both warn explicitly against rapid dose reduction in physically dependent patients.[ref:agnoli-jama-2021][ref:cdc-2022]

At the first visit: complete the full intake assessment, prescribe with documented awareness of the dose and your clinical rationale, and use the consult pathway for pain-management input. A reasonable consult ask: “Patient stable on [X] MME/day for [Y] years. PDMP and UDS reviewed; functional status [description]; concurrent benzodiazepines [yes/no]. Please review current regimen, advise on appropriateness, whether a structured gradual taper is indicated, and whether ongoing co-management is appropriate.”

Counterpoint: when patients agree to taper and it is done gradually (≤10% per month) with behavioral support, outcomes including pain, function, and quality of life can improve; for patients on opioids ≥1 year, tapers take months to years. Avoid the equal-and-opposite error of locking in indefinite continuation without reassessment.[ref:lin-nejm-2025]

faqs.title: The full CDC-aligned first-visit checklist for inherited opiate patients
faqs.first_layer_html:
The four-item intake checklist captures the at-the-moment go/no-go. This is the complete 11-element first-visit framework for the chart, synthesized from CDC 2022, Coffin 2022, and VA/DoD 2022. Address all 11 at the first visit, or document each as deferred with a plan.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:coffin-am-2022][ref:vadod-2022]

#ElementNotes
1Continue regimen absent life-threatening signalsSedation, respiratory depression, slurred speech, or evidence of active diversion = acute safety signals warranting dose change even at the first visit
2MME calculation and documentationSee Morphine milligram equivalents
3PDMP reviewMandatory per-prescription in NY; initial plus quarterly in NJ
4Baseline UDSNon-punitive; see UDS at intake
5Offer naloxoneDocument offer, counseling, and household access
6OUD screenTAPS, DAST-10, or NIDA Quick Screen; apply DSM-5 11-criterion checklist if positive
7Mental-health comorbidity screenDepression, anxiety, PTSD — common co-occurring conditions affecting pain, function, and opioid response
8Functional status and treatment goalsPEG scale (Pain, Enjoyment, General activity); establish baseline and discuss goals of therapy
9Concurrent benzodiazepine checkSee Concurrent opiates and benzodiazepines
10Documentation of continuation rationaleYour clinical rationale for continuing vs. modifying — this is what protects you and the patient
11Follow-up within 1–3 monthsShorter interval (2–4 weeks) for higher-risk regimens (high MME, concurrent benzo, active concerns)

sub_questions.question: Which of these can I reasonably defer past the first visit?
sub_questions.answer_html: The go/no-go safety elements cannot wait: PDMP review, MME documentation, the concurrent-benzodiazepine check, naloxone offer, and screening for acute safety signals. Comorbidity screening and formal functional-goal setting (PEG) can be initiated at the first visit and completed at the 2–4 week follow-up if time is short — but document them as deferred-with-a-plan rather than omitted. The continuation-rationale note is never deferred: if you prescribe, the rationale belongs in that visit’s chart.

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Pain management consultation is appropriate when function is not improving, documentation is limited, or the dose is well above 50 MME/day without clear justification. For suspected OUD, route to addiction medicine rather than pain management.

faqs.title: Inheriting a high-dose patient — continuity, documentation, and the consult
faqs.first_layer_html:
Do not abruptly discontinue or reduce dose at the first visit while awaiting specialist input. Continuity of an established regimen while arranging appropriate oversight is clinically and ethically defensible per CDC 2022 Recommendation 5. The FDA has issued a prescriber warning about the hazards of rapid taper or sudden discontinuation in physically dependent patients — acute withdrawal, pain exacerbation, serious psychological distress, and suicidal ideation.[ref:cdc-2022]

Continuity is conditional on the absence of acute safety signals: sedation, respiratory depression, slurred speech, or evidence of active diversion at the visit. If those are present, dose reduction or discontinuation may be warranted even at the first encounter.

Continuity is a bridge, not an endpoint. The structured benefit–risk reassessment is still the work. Complete all 11 first-visit framework elements (see Complete first-visit framework) and arrange the consult.

sub_questions.question: What is the consult ask at high dose?
sub_questions.answer_html: Be specific: “Patient inherited on [X] MME/day of [agent] for [indication]. Prior pain-management documentation: [present / limited / absent]. PDMP: [findings]. UDS: [confirms prescribed agent / unexpected finding]. Functional status: [PEG scores; brief description of work, ADLs, pain interference]. Concurrent benzodiazepine: [yes/no, dose/indication if yes]. Treatment goals discussed and documented. Please advise: (1) whether the dose is appropriate for the indication, (2) whether a structured gradual taper is indicated and at what rate, and (3) whether ongoing co-management is appropriate.” Where the picture suggests OUD rather than or alongside chronic pain, reframe to “Patient with chronic pain and possible OUD — please advise on MOUD candidacy and transition plan,” and route to addiction medicine.

sub_questions.question: The patient says their prior doctor "always" prescribed this and they'll go elsewhere if I change anything.
sub_questions.answer_html:
Acknowledge the anxiety without making promises: “I understand this medication has been important to your quality of life, and I’m not here to take anything away from you today. I do need to complete my own assessment as your new provider, and I want to make sure we’re doing this in a way that protects you.”

Do not let the threat of departure drive clinical decisions — but do not dismiss it either. Patient distress at the prospect of dose changes is a clinically meaningful signal: it may reflect undertreated pain, anxiety, or features of opioid use disorder, all of which warrant assessment. Document not just the threat but your clinical assessment of what is driving it. CDC 2022 and AAFP are clear: acknowledge the discordance, express empathy, and implement patient-centered changes without abandoning the patient.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:aafp-roth-2020]

PDMP and UDS reviewed; functional status [PEG]; concurrent benzodiazepine [yes/no]. Please advise whether the dose is appropriate, whether a structured gradual taper is indicated and at what rate, and whether ongoing co-management is appropriate.

faqs.title: Concurrent opiates and benzodiazepines — high-risk, but not automatic discontinuation
faqs.first_layer_html:
Do not stop either medication at the first visit for a patient on a long-term, stable concurrent regimen. Withholding the benzodiazepine risks withdrawal seizure; withholding the opioid risks withdrawal and uncontrolled pain. CDC 2022 explicitly warns against abrupt changes that destabilize patients; VA/DoD 2022 cautions against abrupt benzodiazepine discontinuation due to seizure and death risk.[ref:cdc-2022][ref:vadod-2022]

First-visit protocol

  • Continue both medications at current doses
  • Document the combination as a known risk — dose, duration, indication, prior taper attempts, functional status, prior overdose history, household risk
  • Prescribe naloxone — ASAM 2025 makes this a strong recommendation for all patients co-prescribed opioids and benzodiazepines[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo]
  • Plan shorter-interval follow-up: 2–4 weeks rather than 3 months
  • Initiate (not necessarily complete) specialist referral if there is concern about the indication for either medication or if tapering is being considered
  • Reassess benefit–risk at least every 3 months per ASAM 2025, regardless of stability[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo]

How dangerous is the combination? The elevated overdose risk is real but time-dependent. Concurrent opioid–benzodiazepine prescribing is associated with roughly 2–5× increased overdose risk — but a Medicare cohort found HR 5.05 in the first 90 days of concurrent use, dropping to non-significant after 180 days of stable concurrent use. Long-term stable low-dose concurrent regimens carry meaningfully lower risk than newly-started combinations — which is exactly why destabilizing the inherited stable patient is the wrong move. CDC 2022 Recommendation 11 is Category B (“particular caution”), not Category A (“avoid”).[ref:hernandez-jamaopen-2018][ref:sun-bmj-2017][ref:cdc-2022]

sub_questions.question: Can I just taper the benzo now?
sub_questions.answer_html:
Not unilaterally at the first visit. CDC 2022 warns that abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal can cause rebound anxiety, hallucinations, seizures, delirium tremens, and, rarely, death. ASAM 2025 states clinicians “should not discontinue benzodiazepines abruptly in patients who are likely to be physically dependent.” The NEJM review recommends gradual discontinuation over at least 4–8 weeks, with hospitalization considered for very high doses (≥100 mg diazepam-equivalent daily).[ref:cdc-2022][ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo][ref:soyka-nejm-2017]

Keep the tapers separate: do not conduct concurrent opioid and benzodiazepine tapers simultaneously — hold the opioid dose stable through the benzodiazepine reduction period. Sequencing should be individualized; a 2023 scoping review of 26 guidelines found zero provided specific guidance on sequence, and the four that addressed it gave conflicting recommendations.[ref:wang-jcm-2023]

If OUD is present alongside the combination: ASAM 2025 recommends stabilizing on MOUD before initiating a benzodiazepine taper. The OUD pathway takes priority over benzo deprescribing in this subset.[ref:asam-acmt-2025-benzo]

consult_decision_point.prefill_text: Patient on stable concurrent opioid + benzodiazepine regimen ([agents/doses/indications]). Naloxone prescribed. Requesting input on benefit–risk of the combination and, if tapering is indicated, on sequencing — opioid held stable through any benzodiazepine reduction. If OUD is present, advise on MOUD stabilization before benzodiazepine taper.
